$comment: Animal Friends TCG — the First Boroughs collection (AF-MAKER-01), and the only card set the game plays. 'characters' holds one entry per named character: name, species, studies, pronouns, backstory, voice, arc, plus 'wantedVerbs' (effects the story wanted that the engine cannot yet do) and 'wantedArt' (scenes still to be painted). 'cards' are the cards themselves; a 'token' card is a third thing again, declaring that a kind of token exists — one per species, one per study, one for Buildings — rather than being a card anybody draws, and the 'tokens' block below says what they are for. An 'obscured figure' is a fourth thing: a Character the borough never got a name for, carrying `anchor` so that any dearer Character of the same species — or in the same study — may be played over them, whatever their name, which is the ward record being corrected rather than a promotion. The world the writing draws on is docs/TOWN_BIBLE.md. 'rarity' and 'power' are computed by npm run stamp, never hand-written.
name: Maker Cards
blurb: The First Boroughs: ten species, eight studies, eighty-seven named animals — eighteen of whom the borough never got a name for — and the town they all argue in.
note: The whole game is played off this shelf: the two decks above, a deck of your own out of the Deck Workshop, and the one Capital City below.

decks.name: Furrow & Warren
decks.blurb: Rabbits of Agriculture and Civics: the allotment strip, the parish meeting and more of them arriving than leaving. No one Rabbit is much; the sixth one out of your hand is the whole town.

decks.name: Margin & Pantry
decks.blurb: Mice of Lore and Food: the reading room over the kitchen. Every Event the borough has ever filed is played once, fished back out of the dump and played again, and there is always something on the stove.

decks.name: Bench & Bylaw
decks.blurb: Badgers of Crafts and Civics: the bench and the bylaw, and neither of them moves. Whatever the Capital City posts this morning, the work goes on and somebody is put back on the books by lunch.

decks.name: Hedge & Holiday
decks.blurb: Hedgehogs of Agriculture and Entertainment: a hedge laid to last fifteen years and a bank holiday declared on the strength of it. Nothing the rival does reaches anybody in this town.

decks.name: Bin & Barter
decks.blurb: Raccoons of Commerce and Lore: the City Dump is this town’s second hand and its archive. What the other Mayor threw out on Tuesday is on a trestle with a price on it by Thursday.

decks.name: Gavel & Greasepaint
decks.blurb: Foxes of Commerce and Entertainment: they know what the Capital City is about to put up, what it is worth, and how to look like they do not want it. The bid changes after the bidding has opened.

decks.name: Current & Counter
decks.blurb: Otters of Food and Commerce: the counter by the water, open all hours. Work slides from paw to paw, nobody in this town sits down for long, and the round is finished before the rival has finished their Ready.

decks.name: Cache & Kitchen
decks.blurb: Squirrels of Civics and Food: a town that is poor all game and rich exactly once, on the turn it has been saving for. Everything is put by, minuted, and spent at the auction nobody expected them at.

decks.name: Lens & Lathe
decks.blurb: Cats of Science and Crafts: a lens ground to a tolerance nobody asked for, by somebody who was not supposed to be up. This town acts on the turn it feels like acting, and the rival’s Ready can wait.

decks.name: Dome & Dusk
decks.blurb: Owls of Science and Entertainment: the dome, the late hall and a forecast to the minute. An Owl town is wise, awake and poor — so it reads the deck, wakes the shift up early, and is three turns ahead by dawn.

characters.name: Abigail
characters.backstory:
Abigail works the counter at Gwen's, on the corner opposite Bean's, and has since the week she turned up needing a fortnight's work between things and simply never left. She remembers an order without writing it down, she is on a first-name basis with everyone who has ever sat at that counter, and the jar by the register has her name on it more often than the register does — the borough tips her the way it argues about the second post, which is to say constantly and without much heat, because everyone already agrees.

What nobody at the diner knows unless they have also been in the Open Mic Room on a Tuesday is that Abigail taps. Cassadee gave her five minutes on a slow night two years ago on the strength of nothing at all, and Abigail has had a standing slot ever since, between the acts that actually rehearse. She is not, by her own flat assessment, going to be the thing the room remembers about that night. She goes anyway, on her feet after a full shift, because the counter pays the rent and the five minutes is the only thing on her list that is entirely hers.

She is loved out of all proportion to how much she asks for, which is the thing about Abigail that the diner and the open mic room have in common: she shows up, she does the small job in front of her exactly right, and everyone leaves a little more than they meant to.
characters.voice: Warm, quick, unbothered. Talks about the tap classes the way other animals talk about the weather — pleasant, minor, entirely her own business.
characters.arc: No ability at any cost — Abigail's whole trick is doing the ordinary job better than it is asked for, so every version of her simply gathers more Supply than the shift printed for its cost would normally pay.

wantedArt.why: No painted tile shows a diner counter or a tap floor. All four borrow the plain Otter scene until one is commissioned.

characters.name: Adam
characters.backstory:
Adam mends roads. The lane down to the ferry steps, the long pull up to the county gate, the square's cobbles after festival week — all of it is his, and all of it is work nobody notices until it stops being done. He was out on the county road the year the bridge went, and stayed out on it for most of that spring getting carts round the long way.

He is a Badger about it in the ordinary Badger fashion: he starts at one end, he does not hurry, and he is still there at the end of the day when everybody who came to watch has gone home.
characters.voice: Level and unhurried. Talks about a road the way other animals talk about a relative.
characters.arc: The lad with the barrow at 1 and the animal who decides where the road goes at 4. Both cards do nothing but work, because a road is nothing but work; the difference between them is how much of it is his.

wantedArt.why: Adam is a new animal and no painted tile shows this job. With no `art` set the cards fall back to the painted Badger scene, which is the right species doing the wrong work.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_adam_road_mender_1 → the makerworkshop atlas, tile 9; mk_adam_surveyor_of_ways_4 → the makerworkshop atlas, tile 10. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Andrew
characters.backstory:
Andrew keeps the late desk at the Lending Library — the hours after the children's corner has emptied and the last of the evening readers have gone. He locks up after Inkwell's evening and does not go home. What cannot be lent out he copies by hand, a page or two a night, so that there is a second one.

He is an Owl, so the hours suit him and the pay does not. The library has never been able to explain the arrangement to the Counting House and has stopped trying.
characters.voice: Mild, unhurried, apologetic about the hour and plainly delighted by it.
characters.arc: Night Copyist (0) is one desk and one lamp; Keeper of the Late Desk (2) is the whole dark half of the building. An Owl earns almost nothing, and Andrew earns rather less than that, so both cards are small — which is the character, not an oversight.

wantedArt.why: Andrew is a new animal and no painted tile shows this job. With no `art` set the cards fall back to the painted Owl scene, which is the right species doing the wrong work.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_andrew_night_copyist_0 → the makercivic atlas, tile 12; mk_andrew_keeper_of_the_late_desk_2 → the makercivic atlas, tile 13. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Annabelle
characters.backstory:
Everything the borough throws out goes through the Salvage Yard, and everything with words on it goes through Annabelle. She pulls the paper out before the weather gets at it: ward minutes, split almanacs, bills of lading, half a novel, the Grain Exchange's returns for a year nobody can otherwise account for. What is legible she flattens, dries and files. What is not she keeps anyway, on the grounds that she has been wrong before.

She and Beck have an arrangement of long standing and no written terms: she keeps the ones with words on, he gets first read of anything with a story in it, and neither of them has ever had to say so out loud.
characters.voice: Dry, unbothered, faintly amused at what animals throw away.
characters.arc: Paper Sorter (0) is the yard in the rain; Salvage Archivist (3) is the dry shed, the press and the shelves. Neither card does anything clever, because the work is the same work either way and the only thing that changes is how much of it survives.

wantedArt.why: Annabelle is a new animal and no painted tile shows this job. With no `art` set the cards fall back to the painted Raccoon scene, which is the right species doing the wrong work.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_annabelle_paper_sorter_0 → the makerworkshop atlas, tile 11; mk_annabelle_salvage_archivist_3 → the makerworkshop atlas, tile 12. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Baby Mouse
characters.backstory:
The Lending Library's lower shelves are at Baby Mouse height, which is how the borough found out that the lower shelves had been reorganised. Nobody asked for it. It is, annoyingly, better.

Mice do the borough's paperwork and they start early. A Baby Mouse cannot read the ward minutes and can absolutely find them, and Ned has stopped pretending that this is not useful. Three days of fetching adds up to about one Supply and one page filed somewhere nobody will ever look, and both of those are the beginning of a career.

Ned counts the post at two, and has argued it at a meeting. An animal who knows where things are is not an apprentice, he said; an animal who knows where things are is half a clerk already, and the ward record has said so ever since.
characters.voice: Very quiet, and then a fact nobody knew.
characters.arc: A Baby Mouse counts for two when a Mouse is set over them: a season on the lower shelves is half of what any Mouse in this borough can find.

wantedArt.want: Baby Mouse: Lynnette found the missing year of Grain Exchange returns behind the atlases. Lynnette did not find them. A Baby Mouse found them and Lynnette carried them.

characters.name: Badger Cub
characters.backstory:
A Badger Cub is put in the corner of the workshop with a block and a blunt gouge and is not spoken to for a fortnight. This is not neglect; it is the whole of the Badger method, and every Badger in the First Boroughs has been through it. You are given the block. The block is not explained.

It takes three days to get a Supply's worth of anything out of a Badger Cub, and the borough considers that fast. What is being built in the corner is not the block. Badgers start slowly and then do not stop, and a Cub who has sat through the fortnight has already done the hardest part of being a Badger.
characters.voice: Says almost nothing for a very long time, and then says exactly the thing.
characters.arc: The longest apprenticeship in the borough. A Badger Cub counts for two when any Badger is set over them, because half a Badger's training is already done in that corner.

wantedArt.want: Badger Cub: Barrow's first block is still on the shelf above his bench. It is not a good block. He will not have it moved.

characters.name: Barnaby
characters.backstory:
Nobody knows where Barnaby came from, and Barnaby has never once been unhelpful about it — they answer every question pleasantly and afterwards you notice you have learned nothing. They arrived with a ledger case and a hat, they audit the night's books better than anyone in the Capital City, and they are gone before the first shift bell. The Hiring Hall has no address for them. The Counting House has stopped asking.

Two cracks in it. Put an apple pie in front of Barnaby and something goes wrong with them — the hands go still, the voice goes strange, and they will not say why, and they will not eat it, and they will not let anyone take it away either. And mention anime, and you meet a completely different animal: bright, loud, talking with both wings about episodes nobody else in the borough has seen, for as long as you will let them. Then the hat goes back on.

The town has settled on liking them and not prying, which is the most First Boroughs solution possible to a genuine mystery.
characters.voice: Pleasant, precise, entirely uninformative — except on exactly two subjects.
characters.arc: One card only: a Capital City hire who sees further down your deck than anyone and bins what he does not like the look of. The mystery is the flavor; the auditing is the mechanism. His shift is poor — two turns for two — because what you are hiring is the eyes.

wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for 'look at the top 4 and send any you want to the town dump'. `scryDeck` can only put the cards you do not want on the BOTTOM of your deck — nothing in the engine moves a card from your deck to your Town Dump.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Kept the look at four and the choice of which to get rid of, with the unwanted cards going to the bottom of the deck instead of the Dump. The card's text says what it really does. A `binDeckCards` (or a `to: "dump"` option on scryDeck) would be a small engine change and would make this card exactly right.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built. `scryDeck` takes `to: "dump"`, and the card now says what the maker asked for.

characters.name: Barrow
characters.backstory:
Barrow cut stone in the Capital City for twenty years — frontages, stairs, the kind of work that goes up behind hoardings and is admired by animals who will never know your name. He was good at it and it was killing him by inches: too loud, too fast, too many buildings that were finished before he had finished looking at them.

So he came out to the First Boroughs, where the work is smaller and the town is not finished. That is the whole appeal. Barrow wanted to be somewhere still being built — somewhere a wall he sets this spring will still be the wall everyone walks past in thirty years, and somewhere the animals walking past it will know who set it. He is slow to talk, quick to help, and has opinions about foundations that he will share whether or not you have asked.

He bids on every lot that comes up with a roof on it.
characters.voice: Few words, all of them load-bearing. Warms up completely on the subject of mortar.
characters.arc: One card only: a Capital City hire, and the most expensive animal in the game. His whole pull is toward the Capital City's lots — he wins them slightly more often, and pays you for every one that is not a Statue.

wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for an ability that helps you get more Buildings specifically. The engine can only discount a Building through a city rule (`buildingCostDelta`, which only an Ordinance may set), and the only card-level conditions on a Capital City card are `statue` and `nonStatue` — there is no way to say 'a Building' on a Character.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Bid higher and get paid for what you win: `firstBidPlus1` while Barrow is upright, and 1 Supply whenever you gain a non-Statue Capital City card. Buildings are bought at auction like everything else, so this is the nearest honest thing — it just also helps with Market cards.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as a `buildingDiscount` mod, which `cardCostFor` applies to Buildings only. Barrow now makes a Building 1 cheaper at the start of each of your turns.

characters.name: Bean
characters.backstory:
Bean's parents ran the coffeehouse by the Hiring Hall for thirty years, and then retired to the tropics on a Tuesday with four days' notice and a postcard that said 'you'll be marvellous'. Bean was not consulted. Bean has not stopped moving since.

They open before the early shift and they are still wiping down when the night workers come off, and in between they are three orders behind and completely convinced the whole thing is about to come apart. It never quite does. The coffee is good, the room is warm, and every animal in the borough has at some point been got back on their feet by Bean putting something hot in front of them without being asked — which is the one thing Bean does not think of as work, and the one thing the town would miss most.

They keep it open for their parents, who are not coming back, and who would not have minded either way. Peanut keeps the books, works the counter, and takes over on the days Bean is coming apart.
characters.voice: Fast, apologetic, mid-sentence about something else. Calms down entirely while actually making coffee.
characters.arc: The same wake-up-call Owl at 1, 3 and 5, in Food, which is the study the café should always have been.

characters.name: Beck
characters.backstory:
Beck keeps the ward book, lights nothing on fire, and is home by seven. He clerks — bylaws, ward rolls, the lamplighters' hours — and he clerks well, because the work is quiet and nobody needs him to be interesting at it. Ask the Hiring Hall about Beck and you will get a shrug and 'no trouble, ever', which in that room is high praise.

The evening is the part he is actually living for. A candle, a chair, whatever he has got hold of that week, and two or three hours of nothing but reading before bed and the same again tomorrow. He takes in what the borough throws out — a split almanac off the City Dump, somebody's water-stained novel, a bundle of old ward minutes nobody has wanted since the bridge went — and he has read all of it, which is why he is the animal who quietly knows the answer and waits to be asked twice before giving it.

He is not boring. He is simply finished with the day at the end of it. Lynnette has offered him a shelf and he has never taken her up on it; he prefers the ones nobody else wanted.
characters.voice: Quiet, unhurried, slightly reluctant to be the one talking. Says 'well — it's in the book' and then recites it.
characters.arc: Beck reads, and reading pays in cards and in second chances at Events. The Bylaw Reader (1) works a long slow shift and comes back with a card. The Ward Clerk (2) pulls an Event back out of the Town Dump every shift. The Lamplighter's Clerk (3) is the Raccoon signature — on his way home he takes something out of the City Dump that nobody else wanted. The Keeper of the Ward Book (5) is Beck at the end of the arc and exactly as quiet as he was at the start: he has read the whole thing, so his challenge bids win ties, and every shift is another Event back out of the bin. Added since: a Candlelight Reader at 4 who takes a card out of the City Dump off the turn's first Lore Event — the signature hung on the study the whole character is made of.

wantedArt.why: A new job, with no tile of its own. boroughs/3 is the clerk at the lamplighters' desk, which is the cost-3; the Keeper is the same raccoon at home with one candle and the ward book open on his knees.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_beck_keeper_of_the_ward_book_5 → the makercivic atlas, tile 7. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Bella
characters.backstory:
If you cannot find Bella she is in the forest, and if you cannot find her in the forest you are not looking down. She works on the floor of it: knees in the leaf litter, notebook open on one knee, voice recorder in the other paw because some things have to be said before they can be written. She has been at it since she was a kid, when foraging was simply how the family ate through the back half of the year and Bella was the one who came home with a full basket and a list of everything she had walked past on the way.

She never stopped and she never scaled it up. Ecology is what she calls it now, and the Science hall files her recordings and cites them, but the method has not changed since she was seven: go out, sit down, watch one square of ground long enough that it starts telling you things. She can feed herself off a hedgerow in any month of the year and would rather. The whole point, as far as Bella is concerned, is that the woodland was already working before anybody built anything on it, and will still be working after.

That is also her limit. She has never bid on anything in her life, she is no use whatsoever in the Capital City, and she has an audible opinion about animals who would rather raise a building than walk out and look at what is already there. Put Bella in a finished town with everything standing and she is a mouse with a notebook. Put her in a young one, or an empty one, and she is the reason it eats.
characters.voice: Quiet, exact, always slightly mid-sentence. Answers a question with what she saw, the date she saw it, and what the weather was doing.
characters.arc: Every rung is about needing less, and every rung is worth most to a Mayor who has built nothing. Forager (0) makes your next Event need one fewer animal, and pays a bare town outright. Field Scientist (1) turns her own shift into a card, and into Supply while the town has raised at most one thing. Field Recorder (2) puts a spent Event back under the deck; Wildlife Warden (3) puts one straight back in your hand — the Mouse signature, and Bella's whole trick: nothing is used up, it comes round again. Ecologist (5) makes the first Event of every turn cheaper in animals, pays you for playing it, and keeps drawing you cards right up until the eight places start filling. The maker asked for a character strongest when the player has little or nothing built; the cards now say so outright. Added since: a Science Hall Fellow at 4 who buys a Science animal out of Unemployment a Supply cheaper — the citations turned into somebody else's job.

wantedVerbs.verb: buildingsAtMost (a condition on how much the town has built)
wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for Bella's effects to be at their most powerful when the player has little to no buildings. The engine tracks `p.buildings`, but no card condition reads it — `CONDITIONS` has nothing about buildings, statues or town size, so 'while you control no Buildings, gain 2 Supply instead of 1' cannot be written.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Built the same statement out of the one scarcity the vocabulary does read: `eventCharReduction` and the `eventCharReductionPerTurn` passive, which are worth most to a player with few animals standing, and a cost curve weighted to the cheap end so Bella is at her best before a town has raised anything. A `buildingsAtMost` condition would let the cards say it outright.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as the `buildingsAtMost` condition (and `buildingsAtLeast` beside it), which reads the Buildings a town has actually raised — not the Statues, which are bought rather than built. Three of Bella's five rungs now pay extra to a Mayor with nothing up, which is what the maker asked for and what the old `eventCharReduction` reading could only imply.

wantedArt.why: neighbors tile 2 is the Mouse herbalist at a bench of jars, and it reads as Rosabeth's apothecary rather than Bella's. Nothing in any atlas shows an animal sitting in the leaf litter with a notebook and a recorder, which is the whole character. A forest-floor scene would fix all five at once.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_bella_forager_0 → the makerwoodland atlas, tile 8; mk_bella_field_scientist_1 → the makerwoodland atlas, tile 9; mk_bella_field_recorder_2 → the makerwoodland atlas, tile 10; mk_bella_wildlife_warden_3 → the makerwoodland atlas, tile 11; mk_bella_ecologist_5 → the makerwoodland atlas, tile 12. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Benjamin
characters.backstory:
Benjamin makes the borough's lanterns, and he keeps the borough's fire record, and he has never been able to explain to anybody's satisfaction that these are the same job. Light shows us who we truly are, he says, which sounds like a lantern maker being poetic until you watch him do it: he will hold a lamp up to a beam and tell you the year the shed above it burned, who rebuilt it, what they rebuilt it out of, and why the joint is wrong.

The fire is the first half. He has been at it since he was small enough to be carried away from it — a wick, a dish of oil, the blue at the bottom of the flame, the exact moment a lamp catches. The borough has decided this is fine. It is fine because Benjamin is the most careful animal in the First Boroughs about it: he is the one who goes round the sheds in the dry weeks, he is the one who made Morty move the mill's spare oil, and the standing arrangement that the night round's lamps are filled at his bench and nowhere else is his own rule, not the ward's.

The second half is the record. Everything in this town that has ever burned is written down in Benjamin's hand, and because a fire record is really a record of what a place chose to rebuild, he ended up the animal the borough asks about its own history. He works the Town Dump the way other animals work a shelf — a thing thrown out is a thing somebody decided about, and he will go and get it back, and he is nearly always right that it was wanted. Mandee carries his lanterns on the night round, and between the two of them the night shift has never stumbled.
characters.voice: Warm, a little grand, and absolutely serious about light. Starts sentences with "The year that went —". Will not let you leave a lamp where he can see it is wrong.
characters.arc: Five rungs and one flame. The Wick Trimmer at 0 is the Otter keeping others moving. The Lantern Maker at 2 starts going back into the Dump, a card at a time, to the bottom of the deck. The Town Historian at 3 does both halves of his job in one shift — a shift moved, a thing recovered. The Master Lantern Maker at 4 gets it back into his hand instead, and the Keeper of the Light at 5 does it every morning, because by then the record is the town's and not his.

wantedArt.why: The Historian wants the fire book open on a trestle with a lamp held over a burnt beam. It carries neighbors/13, Benjamin's lamplighter portrait, as a stand-in — the right animal, the wrong hour.

wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for a character who can return cards from the Town Dump. The engine only reaches Events there — `eventFromDumpToHand` and `eventFromDumpToDeckBottom` — and the one verb that reaches any card in a bin, `takeFromCityDump`, is the Raccoon's and works the shared City Dump instead. A Market card or a Character in your own Town Dump cannot be got back at all.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Events only, on four of the five rungs — which is the half of the Dump the engine can see. It is also, awkwardly, the Mouse's signature on an Otter, so Benjamin keeps `moveShift` and `readyNextTurn` on the rungs either side of it and reads as an Otter who happens to go through bins.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `cardFromDumpToHand`, which reaches any card of yours in the Town Dump rather than only the Events, with a `filter` for cards that should reach less far. The Master Lantern Maker takes back anything costing 3 or less; the Keeper of the Light takes back anything at all. The narrow verb stays the narrow verb and the two cheap rungs still use it, which is the arc: the bench, then the bin, then the whole record.

characters.name: Berry
characters.backstory:
Berry retired. There was a party, a speech, a clock from the guild, and a plan involving the allotment and a great many naps. The retirement lasted about a fortnight, which everyone who knows Berry had privately predicted, because the trouble with being the animal who can fix it is that the borough knows where you live.

It starts small — somebody's hinge, somebody's pump — and by the spring they are on the committee, and by midsummer they are the one the Town Workshop calls when the clock stops and nobody under fifty can say why. Berry says yes. Berry has never in their long life managed to say the other thing. They arrive with their own tools and a tin of something baked, they work quietly and much faster than anyone expects, and they will not hear a word about payment beyond the tea.

What the town sometimes forgets, because Berry is so kind about it, is that they are the cleverest animal in the First Boroughs. The clock they mended at ninety keeps better time than the one that replaced it. Younger animals come to them for the answer and leave having been gently walked into working it out themselves, which is a harder trick and takes longer, and Berry has all the time in the world for it.
characters.voice: Unhurried, warm, faintly amused. Asks after your family first. Gives the answer as a question so you can have it as your own idea.
characters.arc: Six cards across three studies, and one continuous joke: Berry keeps being pulled back in. Crafts is the bench — Retired Tinker (0) and Workshop Elder (4), the quills-out protection the Hedgehog charter is built on. Science is the mind — Clockmaker (1) orders what is coming, Consulting Engineer (3) makes the next machine pay double. Civics is the part they never volunteered for and cannot get out of — Committee Volunteer (2) drags somebody else back out of Unemployment with them, and Guild Warden (5) does it for free and puts the quills up while they are at it.

wantedVerbs.why: The grandparently half of Berry wants to put the quills around somebody ELSE. `protectCharacter` auto-picks the source Character whenever it is a legal option, and `matchesFilter` has no `notSelf` key (only `advanceCharacter` and `readyNextTurn` handle notSelf, and they do it in their own code).
wantedVerbs.workaround: Berry protects Berry, and shields the whole town from Unemployment at 4 with `unemploymentShield` — which the Hedgehog charter explicitly calls part of the signature.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built. `protectCharacter` honours `filter: { notSelf: true }`, and the Guild Warden puts the quills around somebody else.

characters.name: Betty
characters.backstory:
Betty is Bob's twin sister and got the whole morning's allowance of energy, which the family has never entirely forgiven her for. She whittles, she builds, she grafts, she solders, and about four times a year she blows something up, on purpose, for a client, with a docket. There is no hobby she has not had and very few she has finished, and the barn at the end of the family plot contains all of them at once, in layers.

The blowing up started honestly. Stumps have to come out of a field and there are two ways to do it: a season with a mattock, or a hole, a charge and an afternoon. Betty worked out which one she preferred at about eleven and has been the animal the grange sends for ever since. It paid for the powder, which paid for the fireworks, which is how the borough's Blossom Week got a finale, and it pays for whatever she is halfway through in the barn this month. She takes the odd jobs to fund the exploits. She would say it the other way round and nobody believes her.

Most of it comes to nothing, cheerfully. Some of it does not. The reclaimed strip along the far hedgerow was four seasons of Betty and a great deal of noise, and it is now the best ground in the borough, and she has already sold it and moved on to something else. She is a Hedgehog, so nothing that goes wrong ever actually hurts her; she is Betty, so it never slows her down either. Bob keeps the gate. Betty keeps going through it.
characters.voice: Loud, delighted, already onto the next thing. Explains the interesting part first and the safety part late, if at all.
characters.arc: Six versions and no career, which is the point. The two odd jobs that fund everything sit at the bottom — Barn Sweeper at 0 turns a shift into spending money, Stump Blaster at 2 turns a field into cash and costs her something every time. The two Crafts cards are the hobbies that stuck: the Whittler at 1 with her quills out, the Firework Maker at 3 whom nobody in town is willing to sack. Science at 4 is the powder worked out properly, and pays in cards rather than coins. Agriculture at 5 is the one exploit that came off: four seasons, a great deal of noise, and the best ground in the borough — and she puts the quills around somebody else while she is at it, which is as close as Betty ever comes to sitting still.

wantedArt.why: New job — Agriculture with a charge and a fuse. boroughs/4 is the barn sweeper and townlife/9 is the kite; neither is an animal clearing a field with powder.

characters.name: Biff
characters.backstory:
Biff grew up on the edge of the borough, on the kind of smallholding where you are big before you are old. He was never top of the class and has never once claimed otherwise — he says it about himself before anyone else can, cheerfully, as though it settles the matter. What he had was the shoulders, the legs, and a completely unembarrassed wish for the place to be better than it was.

So he took the constable's job, which nobody else wanted, and turned out to be remarkable at it. Not because he is hard: because he is not. Biff knows every animal on his beat by name and most of them by their parents, and he has worked out over twenty years that a town is not made safer by taking animals out of it. He stops the trouble — he is a Hedgehog and he is immovable and the trouble does stop — and then he walks the troublemaker home, and a week later he has found them something to do.

Animals who came up before him have run out of ways to explain that this is not how policing is supposed to work. Biff listens politely to all of them. The beat has the lowest trouble in the First Boroughs, and he does not think it is because of anything clever he did.
characters.voice: Plain, friendly, a bit loud. Calls everyone by name. Apologises for the interruption before stopping you.
characters.arc: Two constables, one career. Beat Constable (2) is Biff on the lane: he comes down it and one of the rival's animals goes back to work. Chief Constable (4) is Biff after twenty years: two of them go back to work, and then he finds a job for somebody who has not got one — at the going rate; Biff finds you the job, he does not pay your wages. `makeBusy` never touches an animal mid-shift, never one pledged into an auction and never one behind a Hedgehog's quills, which is the whole of Biff's method: he stops you, he does not take anything from you. Added since: a Cadet Constable at 0 with nothing on it at all — the year he was learning the names and not yet allowed to use them.

wantedVerbs.verb: a one-sided `makeBusy` / advance-backwards on an opponent's Character
wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for abilities that make an OPPONENT'S Characters busy. Nothing in the engine turns a Character back toward Busy: `advanceCharacter` only turns toward upright, and the only way to reach across the table at all is `unemployOpponentCharacter`, which takes the animal's job away.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Used `blockNextReady`, which stops every Character in BOTH towns advancing at the next Ready — the rival's animals stay down a turn longer, which is the effect asked for, and it is the established pattern (Inkwell, Velvet). Taking a job away was ruled out as the opposite of what Biff is for; that it costs Biff's own town the same turn is the reading the backstory wanted anyway.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `makeBusy`: turns an opponent's Character one step away from upright. It keeps advanceCharacter's manners — never a Character mid-shift, never one pledged, never one behind a Hedgehog's quills. Both of Biff's cards now use it instead of blockNextReady.

characters.name: Bob
characters.backstory:
Bob and Betty were born the same wet morning at the far end of the borough, and between them they were issued exactly one animal's worth of energy. Betty took it. Bob has been tired ever since. He is not unwell and he is not unhappy; he is simply a hedgehog who has never once in his life been fully awake at the hour somebody wanted him to be.

The county gate solved him. It is a post nobody else would take, because its whole duty is saying no — no carts after six, no barrows without a docket, no you cannot just this once. Bob is a Hedgehog. He is immovable, he is unembarrassable, and he can say no in his sleep, which is the arrangement the county and Bob have quietly come to. Carters who arrive at the wrong hour find the bar down and a hedgehog folded against it like a dropped coat, and neither the bar nor the hedgehog is going anywhere until morning.

The difficulty is the other half of the job. A gate has to open as well, and Bob is unbeatable at keeping the borough out and only intermittently good at letting it back in. There is a standing complaint at the Hiring Hall about the mail cart, three separate ones about the fish. It has never come to anything, because everyone who has ever tried to get past him at night agrees that nobody else could have kept them out either.
characters.voice: Short. Slow. Mostly the word 'no', and usually a good while after the question.
characters.arc: One animal, hired out of the Capital City, and one joke in three parts. On display he is the bar across the road for everybody: nobody gets a pledge in cheaply while Bob is on the door, and the only way past him is to hire him. Hired and awake, the bar is still down but it is down on the rival's road — they cannot improve a bid once it is made, because the animal at the gate is not interested in second thoughts. Hired and asleep — Busy, which he is the turn he arrives and every turn he works — everyone gets through, including the ones he was hired to stop. `requiresUpright` is the whole character.

wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for an animal who makes market items harder to buy for BOTH Mayors while he is sitting on the board, and only harder for the rival once he is hired. The second half exists; the first does not. `cityRule()` in src/engine/state.js walks state.market.city but skips every card whose type is not `ordinance`, so a `displayed` ability on a hired animal — `buildingCostDelta`, `statueCostDelta`, `pledgeLadderDelta`, `noRaises` — is read by nothing and would be a silent no-op.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Built only the hired half: a `blockOpponentBidRaise` passive gated on `requiresUpright`, so the rival cannot raise a pending bid while Bob is awake in your town. Nothing happens while he is on display. The gap is exactly one line — letting `cityRule()` read `displayed` abilities on displayed marketCharacters too — but that is engine work and not this card's to do.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built. `cityRule()` now reads `displayed` abilities on displayed marketCharacters as well as Ordinances, so Bob works the door while he is still on the board: every pledge in every auction costs a rung more until somebody hires him out of the way. Buying him is buying the gate — and then it is only shut for the other Mayor.
wantedVerbs.note: The power model does not price a `displayed` ability — every Ordinance rates 0 — because a city rule is a symmetric tax rather than a benefit to whoever owns the card. Bob's rating of 4.70 is therefore his hired half only, and the gate he keeps on the board is free.

characters.name: Brett
characters.backstory:
Brett practises in the Capital City, where the fees are the size of a small town's year and the waiting room has its own waiting room. He does not live in the First Boroughs and has never pretended he might. He comes out when the borough needs somebody who knows exactly how the Capital City's rules are written — which lots may be challenged, which tie goes to whom, what the word 'pending' is actually doing in a clause — argues it, wins it, bills for it, and takes the evening coach home.

The town has complicated feelings about this. He is expensive, he is faintly amused by all of them, and he has never once lost them a lot they asked him to take. The Counting House budgets for him a year ahead. Oatmeal, who does the same work for a ward salary and no applause, is professionally polite to him and privately unimpressed.

He is the other half of Barrow's story: the same big city, the opposite decision. Barrow came out and stayed because the town was still being built. Brett comes out, does the work better than anyone available, and goes back.
characters.voice: Dry, fast, expensive. Explains the rule once, then explains what the rule is for, and the second explanation is the one that wins.
characters.arc: One card, and deliberately the top of the ladder: a Capital City hire at the highest cost in the game, retained for three of your turns and then gone. He works hard while he is here — a full master's shift — because there is no second season of Brett. What you buy is the ties and the challenge income, for as long as the retainer runs. At two turns the model rated him 3.46 and no Mayor would ever have hired him; at three he sits at 5.81, against 5.19 for a comparable animal who never leaves.

wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for a lawyer hired TEMPORARILY. A Character hired out of the Capital City moves into your town and stays there for the rest of the game; nothing in the engine gives a Character a term, a contract length or an exit. Only Limited Events expire (`duration`).
wantedVerbs.workaround: Delivered the 'hired from the big city' half, which is real — he is a Capital City hire, not a townsfolk — and put the temporariness in the backstory and flavor. The nearest true mechanism would be a Limited Event ('Brett's Retainer', 2 turns of his courtroom passives) instead of, or alongside, the Character; that is a card of its own rather than another rung of Brett, so it is the maker's call.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `leavesAfter` on the card: the hire arrives with a term, it ticks down at the end of each of its Mayor's turns, and when it runs out they go back to the Capital City. Brett is retained for two turns.

wantedVerbs.why: His help is meant to be civic — the town's case, not any purchase. `winTiesAsChallenger` applies to every challenge you make.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Left it untyped, as the other cards that use this passive are.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Not built: a challenge is made on a Capital City lot, and a lot has no study to type the bonus by. The Building discount Barrow got is the nearest thing the Capital City can express, and it belongs to a stonecutter rather than a lawyer.

characters.name: Brooke
characters.backstory:
Brooke went onto the Dock rope gang at fourteen and has been working her way up the river trade ever since, which is the thing she would tell you if you asked. The ladder is a real one — dock hand, ferry hand, lighterman, wright — and at the top of it is the licence every otter on the water wants: River Otter, the rank that lets an animal take a loaded boat down the whole river alone, on its own word, with nobody sitting behind it. Brooke has been about two years off it for something like eight years.

The reason is that Brooke cannot hear about a thing without going to find out how it is done. A balloon came over the estuary in her second year and she was at the field before it had finished deflating, and she came back three months later able to fly it. The regatta needed somebody to call the starts, so she learned to call the starts, and then learned the river's whole history because half the calling is knowing whose great-grandmother won which cup. Somebody said, once, that she would never understand a hull until she had built one. She built one. It took four years and it is still on the water and it is the best boat on the river, and it put her licence back by four years.

The docks keep her post open. They have worked out what everyone else works out eventually: Brooke always comes back, and she always comes back able to do something nobody asked her to learn, and sooner or later the river needs it. She will make River Otter. Probably not this year. Somebody has just mentioned the railway.
characters.voice: Cheerful, fast, already halfway out the door. Answers a question with a better question. Says 'right — how does that work, then' more than anything else.
characters.arc: Five careers, one unfinished one. The Commerce card at 1 is the ladder she is actually on, and the tempo verb the Otter charter is built from — she hands the work along and it keeps moving. Lore at 2 is the ferry, where the shift itself changes paws. Entertainment at 3 is the regatta, the one job where her detours pay at once: she gets the whole river back on its feet. Science at 4 is the balloon, kept exactly as it was because it is the best thing she ever did by accident — from up there she can see what the Capital City is about to put up for sale. Crafts at 5 is the boat: four years, one hull, and the thing that finally makes an argument with her expensive. She still is not a River Otter. Added since: a Mooring Hand at 0 with no ability — the rope on the bollard, the bottom rung of the ladder to River Otter.

wantedArt.why: The Regatta Caller is a new job — Entertainment, on a starting barge with a horn. No atlas tile shows it; neighbors/12 is the ferry and would be the wrong animal at the wrong end of the river.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_brooke_regatta_caller_3 → the makerfield atlas, tile 2. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Bunny
characters.backstory:
There is never one Bunny. There is a Bunny, and then there are five more of them coming round the end of the Allotment Strip, and the borough has long since given up counting. The warren's smallest are put on the light rows the moment they can carry a trug — not because anybody needs the help, but because a Rabbit who has not been given a row spends the afternoon in somebody else's.

A Bunny is not much of a worker yet. Three days of a Bunny is about one animal's morning. What a Bunny is, is a place at the Hiring Hall with a name on it, kept warm until whoever grows into it comes to claim it, and in the First Boroughs that has always been worth more than the morning.
characters.voice: All questions, none of them waiting for the answer.
characters.arc: A Bunny is the bottom of every Rabbit's ladder: no rank, no trade, and a post that any Rabbit in the borough may step into as an upgrade.

wantedArt.want: Bunny: Clover gave one a row of its own the summer the beds went in, and by August there were nine rows and no way of saying which Bunny had which.

characters.name: Cassadee
characters.backstory:
Open mic nights in the First Boroughs happen in whatever room will have them, and Cassadee is the animal who decides which room. She books it, sweeps it, sets the chairs, finds the lamp oil, stands at the back with the list, and puts the chairs away again at midnight. She does not sing, play, recite or juggle, and has turned down every invitation to try.

Oatmeal's band is on her list more often than anybody, which she says is because they turn up on time and not because there are five of them and four are brothers and sisters.
characters.voice: Brisk, kind, immovable about the running order. Says 'you are on at nine' as though it were a law.
characters.arc: Two rungs of the same evening: the animal carrying the chairs in at 0, and the animal whose room it is at 3. Nothing on either card but the work, which is the point — the show is somebody else's, and Cassadee is what it stands on.

wantedArt.why: Cassadee is a new animal and no painted tile shows this job. With no `art` set the cards fall back to the painted Hedgehog scene, which is the right species doing the wrong work.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_cassadee_stage_hand_0 → the makercivic atlas, tile 10; mk_cassadee_hall_manager_3 → the makercivic atlas, tile 11. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Clover
characters.backstory:
Clover comes from a gardening family in the plainest sense: four generations on the same allotment strip, and an unbroken line of animals who could tell you what was wrong with a plant by looking at it and could not have told you why. Clover could do the looking by the time they were six. What nobody in the family expected was the other half — the notebook, the labelled rows, the two identical beds planted differently on purpose to see what happened. Clover's grandmother called it fussing. Clover kept fussing.

The fussing turned into botany, which in the First Boroughs means the animal everyone sends for when something green is behaving strangely, and the animal the Science hall sends for when something green has to survive somewhere it has no business surviving. That is how a gardener from the allotments ended up in the glasshouse, and then in the cold rooms, and then — there is a photograph of this in the Lending Library — in a rocket, holding a tray of seed potatoes and looking extremely pleased.

Clover has never once gone anywhere alone. It is not nerves; it simply does not occur to them that a thing worth doing is worth doing by yourself. Every strange place Clover has been talked their way into has had somebody else in the doorway behind them, usually somebody young, usually somebody who had not been asked yet and said yes anyway. Half the borough's gardeners started as the friend Clover brought along.
characters.voice: Curious, unhurried, generous with credit. Says 'come and look at this' before saying what it is. Asks who else is coming.
characters.arc: The same five jobs, deepened: the family's allotment (0), the Saturday stall that pays for the seed (2), the community plot (3), the glasshouse that got them off the ground (4), and the master botanist the whole borough owes a cutting to (5). Two things run the whole way up and they are the two the maker asked for — Supply above what the shift pays, and never arriving alone. At 0 the friend comes out of hand for free; at 3 the friend comes with a coin; at 4 the friend can be a better one; at 5 they bring somebody and the garden pays every morning besides. Both of Clover's Events come with them. Added since: a Plot Sharer at 1 who pays the moment they arrive in a town that already gardens — the gardeners Clover brought along, finally on the card.

wantedVerbs.why: The story wants the friend Clover brings along to arrive able to do something — to land upright, or to bring a Supply of their own. `recruitFromHand` takes an `orientation` and a cost filter and nothing else, so the friend is always just a body entering Busy.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Paid for the friend on Clover's side instead: the Supply is gained by Clover's Mayor in the same ability, which is the same total and reads as Clover covering the seed.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `then`: an effect `recruitFromHand` runs only when a Character actually came out of hand. Clover's Supply is now the seed money for whoever came, not a payment that arrives whether or not anybody did — which is what a `seq` could not say.

characters.name: Comet
characters.backstory:
Comet has wanted to be an astronaut since she was old enough to say the word, and unusually for an animal who wants something that badly, she has never once been talked out of it or distracted from it. She read every book the Lending Library had, then wrote to the Observatory until they let her sweep it, then took the Crafts hall's engine course twice because she did not think she had understood it the first time. She had. She wanted to be sure.

The problem has always been her paws. Comet is clumsy in a way that is genuinely remarkable to watch — she has put a foot through a wing panel, upended a tray of instruments into a fuel tank, and once ended a test by falling out of the machine before it left the ground. The selection board turned her down twice. She did not argue either time; she went away, learned the part they had marked her down on until she knew it better than the board did, and came back.

What she has instead of hands is a head. Comet knows what the Capital City is going to put up for sale before the Capital City has finished deciding, because she has read the manifests, the dock lists and the Observatory's own order book, and she is the animal the whole Science hall asks before anyone bids on anything. She got the seat on the third application. She fell over on the way to the launch. She went anyway, which is the only thing about Comet that has ever needed explaining and the one thing that never does.
characters.voice: Precise, earnest, faintly out of breath. Corrects herself mid-sentence. Apologises for the noise, not for the mess.
characters.arc: Three jobs, one climb, and the Cat signature at the top — Comet goes when she should not be able to. The sharp end of the arc is her head for altitude. At 1 the mechanic's finished job discounts the next thing you build; at 3 the test pilot comes down knowing what the Capital City is about to offer; at 5 the astronaut sees three cards deep and is paid for looking. Added since: a Bolt Sorter at 0 with no ability — the hangar floor, long before the selection board.

characters.name: Cookie
characters.backstory:
Cookie bakes for the Winter Stores. Everything that comes off her board is made to keep: hard biscuit, twice-baked rusk, seed cake that improves for a month and is edible for a year. She uses the Community Oven like everybody else, on the late heat after the bread is out, which is the cool slow end nobody else wants and exactly the end she needs.

She is a Squirrel and the Winter Stores are the largest cache in the borough, so the arrangement was more or less inevitable. She has never eaten anything she baked in the year she baked it.
characters.voice: Practical, warm, slightly stern about dates. Gives you one and tells you not to open it yet.
characters.arc: Biscuit Maker (0) is the corner of somebody's board; Winter Stores Cook (3) is the whole late heat and the Stores' shelves behind it. Neither card does anything on the turn it lands, which is a fair description of Cookie's entire trade.

wantedArt.why: Cookie is a new animal and no painted tile shows this job. With no `art` set the cards fall back to the painted Squirrel scene, which is the right species doing the wrong work.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_cookie_biscuit_maker_0 → the makerharvest atlas, tile 14; mk_cookie_winter_stores_cook_3 → the makerharvest atlas, tile 15. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Copper
characters.backstory:
Copper keeps the borough's weights and measures, and has never in his life spent a coin he could put away instead. This is not meanness — ask anyone he has quietly carried through a bad quarter — it is a settled conviction that something is coming. He does not say what. He has never said what. He simply believes, with the calm of an animal who has thought it through, that the town is one bad winter from finding out how little it set aside, and that somebody had better be ready.

The cellar under the weights office is the proof. It has been filling since he was an apprentice: salt, lamp oil, candle stock, a shelf of small coin nobody has counted but Copper. Twice now the borough has had exactly the kind of season he stocked it for — the year the bridge went, and the winter the Grain Exchange shut for six weeks — and both times the animals who knew about the cellar came and asked, and both times Copper said the same thing. Not yet. This is bad. There will be worse. He lent them the salt on the quiet and did not open the shelf.

What this makes him, at the market, is the cheapest animal in the borough to do business with. Copper has read every schedule of fees the Capital City prints and knows which of them can be got round; he buys at the bottom of the day, rehires at the bottom of the month, and has a way of announcing a price so mild that the room takes a moment to notice it was a price. He is not chasing a bargain. He is building the cellar, and the bargains are just how far his coin goes.
characters.voice: Quiet, mild, apologetic about numbers. Says 'not yet' and 'we'll see' and means both. Never raises his voice and never rounds up.
characters.arc: Five versions, one unopened cellar. The Penny Counter at 0 carries the Cat signature — Copper gets up when he should not, because he has remembered something he did not put away. The middle three are the cellar at ordinary scale: the next animal recruited costs less (1), anything that takes Supply off you is answered out of the shelf (2), and the first price he names each turn is a penny under what it should be (3). The Market Steward at 5 is all of it at once and answers a raid with two. The shelf itself has still never been opened. Added since: a Cellar Keeper at 4 with no ability — the cellar as plain stock rather than as a trick, and the arc's only rung that simply pays.

wantedVerbs.verb: a trigger that fires when Supply is taken from you
wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for effects that RECOVER lost Supply. Nothing in the engine notices a loss as it happens: there is no `onSupplyLost`, so a card cannot say 'whenever an opponent takes Supply from you, take half of it back'. `lossShield` prevents the loss instead, which is a different promise and reads as caution rather than recovery.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Both halves, separately. `lossShield` on the cost-2 is the cellar stopping the loss, and `onChallengedByOpponent → gainSupply` on the cost-5 is the nearest thing the engine has to being paid back for a raid — the one moment a rival reliably costs you Supply and the game tells the card about it.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as the `onSupplyLost` trigger: it fires for the Mayor who actually lost Supply, to a rival's effect or to the weather, and never for a loss of nothing. A card that answers a loss by causing one does not cascade. Copper's cellar now opens exactly when the maker's story said it would — the cost-2 puts back 1, the Market Steward puts back 2 — and `lossShield` went back to being somebody else's idea of caution.

wantedVerbs.why: 'Saving for a rainy day' is literally the Squirrel's signature — caching Supply on a card, safe from shared shocks, to be spent later — and it is exactly Copper's cellar. It is off-limits here: spec/species.json gives `storeSupply` to Squirrels as the one thing only they do, and handing it to a Cat blurs two species for the sake of one joke.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Built the cellar as discounts and shields rather than as a cache. Copper's Supply is not put by, it simply goes further — which is the same story from the other end, and leaves the Squirrels their verb.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Not built, and now not needed. The cellar went onto the town cards instead, where no species charter is at stake: the Emergency Reserve puts 3 Supply by, and Winter Stores hands back everything your Characters have put by the moment something takes Supply off you. Copper drew up the list; the borough opens the door. `storeSupply` stays the Squirrel's.

characters.name: Daisy
characters.backstory:
Daisy is the borough's florist and a hopeless romantic in the full, unembarrassed sense of the word. She knows every scent in the hedgerow by name, she can tell you what a posy is saying and what the animal who ordered it thinks it is saying, and she has sold flowers to most of the couples in the First Boroughs at one end of things or the other.

Her own life is entirely ahead of her. Daisy is waiting to be swept off her feet — properly, without warning, by somebody who turns up at the stall and means it — and she has been waiting cheerfully for years, which the borough finds either lovely or maddening depending on who you ask. In the meantime she sweeps the petals up at the end of the day and dries them, because a Squirrel does not throw away anything that will keep, and the night-bloom stock and the wedding trade and the Festival Green garlands all come out of what she put by in the quiet months.

Festival week is hers. Every garland on the square, every buttonhole in the hall, four days of no sleep, and a full year's takings in one go — which is exactly how a Squirrel likes to be paid.
characters.voice: Bright, dreamy, faster than you expect. 'Don't tell me — no, don't — is it for her?'
characters.arc: Everything Daisy does is put by now and spent all at once later. The Petal Sweeper (0) dries what falls. The Bouquet Weaver (2) looks three cards down the deck for the one she is hoping for. The Night-Bloom Florist (3) works the dark and puts by double. The Festival Florist (4) is the week itself: four days of garlands, and every coin the whole town has stored taken in at the end of it.

wantedVerbs.verb: pairCharacters (two Characters in a town who are worth more to each other)
wantedVerbs.why: Daisy's whole story is the sweeping-off-her-feet that has not happened yet, and the card wanted to notice the animal she is standing next to.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Left as the Squirrel's storage thread — she puts by, and the Festival pays out — with the romance carried in the flavor. `otherCharacterInTown` can name one animal, but Daisy does not know who it is yet, which is the point of her.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `pairCharacters`: Daisy and one other animal are worth 1 more to each other on every shift either of them works, for as long as both keep standing in the town. The bond is read back through the partner rather than promised, so it lapses on its own the moment one of them is unemployed, upgraded away or sent home — which is the other half of the sweeping-off-her-feet that has not happened yet.

characters.name: Daniel
characters.backstory:
Daniel draws the maps and does not go. They have charted the canal from the ferry steps to the county line, the roads out past the toll gate, the coast they have never smelled and, on clear nights from a window, the stars; and the furthest they have been from the borough in their life is the far hedgerow, once, with somebody else.

It is not that they do not want to. It is that they want to enormously, in the abstract, from a desk, with the door shut. A map is the whole adventure with none of the going: the routes, the distances, the marginal note about where the bank shelves and which inn will take a mouse after dark, all of it true and all of it happening to somebody else. Traders come back from the Capital City road and Daniel debriefs them for two hours, corrects the chart, rolls it up, and sleeps in their own bed.

The borough gets a great deal out of this. Everything Brooke's lightermen run by, everything the Science hall's surveys are laid over, and every apprentice sent out to somewhere they have never been with a sheet in their paw and a mouse's careful handwriting on it — all Daniel's, and every one of those animals has been somewhere Daniel has not.
characters.voice: Soft, exact, endlessly curious about elsewhere. 'And what was it like, past the second lock? No — tell me properly.'
characters.arc: Daniel's cards are the route known before the journey: the Event costs one animal fewer, and the top of the deck arrives in the order they charted. Ink Mixer (0) is the desk and the discount. Canal Cartographer (2) adds the chart itself. Star Charter (3) is the window and the night sky, and takes a Character off the Event while they are working. Master Cartographer (4) is the whole wall of maps — the deck in the order they want and a look at what the Capital City is bringing out next, which is as close as Daniel gets to leaving. Added since: a Chart Copier at 1 with no ability — the tracing itself, which has no decisions in it.

characters.name: Dirt
characters.backstory:
Dirt and Squirt are twins and they teach at the borough school, one room each, and the borough has never been certain which of them is in which. This is deliberate. They swap on Tuesdays for no reason, they swap in the middle of a lesson for a better one, and they have twice swapped during a ward meeting while a motion was being read.

Dirt has the upper room and the longer patience. He is the one who will let a bad answer sit in the air for a while, which the kittens find unbearable and which works. Nobody at the school has ever got a straight account out of him about the Tuesdays.

Out of hours he carves and paints figurines — the borough's cast, an inch and a half tall, one at a time, and they take him a season each. Ned has eleven of them on the ward-record shelf. There is no figurine of Dirt. There is a figurine labelled DIRT and it is unmistakably Squirt, and it has been on Ned's shelf for four years, and Dirt has never corrected it.
characters.voice: Slow, dry, and leaves the gap open a beat too long on purpose.
characters.arc: Every version of him is the same trick from a different room: the post stays, the twin in it changes. The cheap ones swap; the dear ones swap and have a season's work put by.

wantedArt.want: Every version of Dirt.

characters.name: Dylan
characters.backstory:
Dylan holds the River Otter licence, which is the thing half the docks are working toward and which he has had since he was absurdly young. He will not tell you how. He will tell you a story about how, and it will be a very good story, and it will be different the next time, and somewhere in the third or fourth telling you will notice that he has never once actually said.

He comes up the river on no schedule anybody has established, ties up, and within an hour is the most talked-about animal in the borough. The tales are the point: the tide that ran backwards, the cargo he will not describe, the winter he spent somewhere with no name. Half the borough is a little in love with him and the other half is pretending not to be. He is warm to everyone, promises nothing to anyone, and has broken no hearts on any account the Registrar can find, which several animals regard as suspicious in itself.

The thing the borough has slowly worked out about Dylan, under all of it, is that he is not actually playing with anyone. Ask him for help — plainly, out loud, for something real — and he puts the story down mid-sentence and does it, and does it better and faster than the animal who asked could have. Then he is gone again, usually before the week is out, and the next anyone hears is a rumour off a barge. Brooke has met him twice and has taken notes both times.
characters.voice: Low, unhurried, amused. Answers a direct question with a better story. The one time he is plain is the one time it matters.
characters.arc: One hired animal, because that is what he is — he is never in a town long enough to have versions. He arrives already able to do the Otter's whole trick: the work slides off whoever is carrying it onto whoever is free, and somebody is up and about tomorrow who had no business being. And then the term runs out and he goes back to the river, which is the only honest way to print him.

characters.name: Earl
characters.backstory:
Earl keeps the tea house, which is not the café and never has been. Bean's counter by the Hiring Hall has the mornings and the accounts and the noise; Earl has the long afternoons, when an animal who needs to sit down with somebody for two hours comes and sits down with somebody for two hours. The two of them have never competed for an hour in their lives and Earl buys his leaf through Bean's supplier, which he will tell you is the only sensible arrangement in the borough.

There are two Earls and the difference between them is a pot of tea. The first one — the afternoon one, the one with a cup already poured — is the calmest animal in the First Boroughs. He listens for an hour without moving, says one thing at the end of it, and animals go away and act on the one thing. The second Earl is what is there before the first cup: fast, loud, four jobs at once, halfway up a ladder with the urn in one paw, talking through a plan that has three steps too many in it. That Earl gets an enormous amount done. That Earl also once reorganised the entire back room at four in the morning, on his own, and could not find anything in it for a fortnight.

What both Earls do is push animals up. He has a thing about it — he cannot watch somebody be good at a job and stay in it. Half the borough's apprentices have been talked into the next thing across his counter, usually over a pot they did not pay for, and when it is genuinely a coin-toss whether an animal is ready he will lean on it, hard, in favour of ready. He has been wrong perhaps four times. He counts them. He will tell you all four if you have an afternoon.
characters.voice: Two speeds and nothing in between. With tea: slow, warm, one sentence at a time. Without: three sentences at once, all of them started. Says 'right — next thing' at both speeds.
characters.arc: Four rungs of the same push, and the tea decides how hard. The Tea Boy at 0 hands a note over with the tray and the next upgrade costs less. The Tea Trader at 2 does it every shift. The Coffee Roaster at 3 is Earl off the tea entirely, frantic at the roaster at four in the morning — and when the room stalls on an even call, that is when he leans hardest. The Tea House Keeper at 4 is the afternoon at its best: he is back on the floor with a cup already poured, and the next animal you push up a rung comes cheap.

wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for a favourable coin flip before Earl helps anybody upgrade: the toss is whether the animal is ready, and Earl leans on it.
wantedVerbs.workaround: The one genuine coin toss the engine already has: the tied bid. `onTiedBid` fires exactly when two Mayors have put up the same number and neither is right, which is the situation Roger is for, and everything he does hangs off it. It is chance the players walked into rather than chance he can call on demand.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `coinFlip`, the same verb Roger asked for. Earl leans on his where the story put it: the Coffee Roaster tosses when he finishes a shift, and heads is the favourable call — the upgrade rate — while tails is the Supply he would have made anyway. An even call about whether an animal is ready, settled the way the borough settles one.

characters.name: Eric
characters.backstory:
Eric was six when he told his parents he was going to be a farmer. His parents are lawyers — Capital City lawyers, the kind the Counting House budgets for a year ahead — and the borough fully expected a row. There was no row. They took him at his word, the way they would take a client at their word, and then they did what that family does with a thing once it has been decided: they bought the best of it. The best agricultural schools. The county-fair circuit every summer from when he was nine. A shelf of seed catalogues that arrived in the post like briefs.

And then, because neither of them could bear to be the least informed animal in a room, they learned it alongside him. His mother can judge a fleece and has the rosettes to prove it. His father reads the almanac cover to cover the week it comes off Lynnette's press and argues with the planting tables in the margin. All three of them show at the county fair and all three of them are a nuisance to beat.

What Eric actually turned out to be good at is not growing things, though he grows things very well. It is knowing what an animal costs to keep for a season, to the Supply, and being willing to say so out loud in front of them. He hires cheaply and he hires well, and nobody has ever accused him of hiring meanly, because the figure he says out loud is the figure he pays and it is usually better than the one they were going to ask for. The borough's wage rates are compared against Eric's, and the grange has quietly stopped arguing with him about it.
characters.voice: Plain, unhurried, and full of numbers he is not showing off about. Says what a thing costs before he says whether he wants it. Calls his parents "the lawyers" with enormous affection.
characters.arc: Five rungs up a farm the lawyers paid for. The Smallholder at 1 knows one animal's keep and shaves it off the next hire. The Fair Steward at 2 learned the trick on the circuit, where you price everything. The Row Farmer at 3 is the Rabbit's own verb — he brings somebody along, and the next hire is cheaper for it. The Row Boss at 4 runs a rate every morning; the Best Farmer There Ever Was at 5 runs it at double, which is what the schooling was for.

wantedArt.why: The top of the arc is Eric and both lawyers in the ring at the county fair with the rosette. It carries boroughs/8, the Row Farmer's field, as a stand-in: nothing in any atlas shows the top of Eric's arc.

wantedVerbs.verb: a standing recruitDiscount that is not spent by the first recruit
wantedVerbs.why: The story wanted a rate — every animal you hire while Eric is standing there costs 1 less — because that is what "he knows what an animal costs to keep" means. `recruitDiscount` is consumed whole by the first recruit it applies to (`consumeModFor`), so it can only ever say "your next recruit".
wantedVerbs.workaround: A discount re-issued every turn: the Row Boss at 4 and the Best Farmer at 5 each hand one out at the start of your turn, so a Mayor who hires once a turn gets the rate and one who hires twice does not.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `townRecruitDiscount`, a passive carrying a value, read by `recruitCost` through `passiveTotal` and never spent by anybody. Eric's two top rungs are rates rather than re-issued discounts now — 1 less on every hire at the Row Boss, 2 at the Best Farmer There Ever Was — and they stop the moment he sits down, because a rate is a thing an animal is standing there saying. The cheap rungs keep their one-off discounts, so the arc reads discount, discount, rate.

characters.name: Faustus
characters.backstory:
Faustus is the loudest animal in any room he is measuring, and he is usually measuring. He is a threadmaster of all types — cloth, canvas, cord, the awful modern stuff the Science hall sends over in sealed tins — and the trick everybody knows him for is that you do not bring him a drawing. You tell him what you want it to look like. You describe it, badly, waving, and he watches your paws rather than your face, and by the time you have finished the sentence he has the bolt down off the shelf and is cutting.

What that has made him, in a town that settles everything by auction, is a fixture of the auction room. Festival week, the regatta, the big lots at the Auction House: Faustus dresses the bidders, and he dresses them on the understanding that he will be in the room to see it. He has opinions about what a well-cut coat does to a bidding war and they are not modest opinions and they are, annoyingly, correct. A Mayor who turns up to the Capital City in something Faustus made has already cost everybody else a rung before anybody has said a number, and the Auction House has quietly stopped pretending otherwise.

He is a Cat, which means all of this happens exactly when it suits him and not a moment before, and he has walked out of a fitting because the light was wrong. Daisy does the flowers for festival week and Faustus does the coats, and the two of them have an arrangement about the square that neither will describe as a friendship.
characters.voice: Loud, delighted, endlessly specific about fabric. Interrupts. Calls everybody "darling" and means it about half the time.
characters.arc: Five rungs, all of them pointed at the auction room. The Bolt Boy at 0 is paid to be in the room when you announce. The Pressure-Suit Tailor at 1 makes a challenge cheaper; the Costumier at 2 makes it win ties. The Sailmaker at 3 is the Cat signature — he gets up when it suits him. The Threadmaster at 5 is the whole thing said out loud: while he is on display in the Capital City, every pledge in every auction costs a rung more, for everybody, and the Mayor who finally hires him gets the first bid of the turn as well.

wantedArt.why: The Threadmaster is a hire out of the Capital City, at the Auction House door in something he made this morning. It carries whiskerwood/3, the quilting bench, as a stand-in — the job he was promoted out of.

wantedVerbs.verb: a pledge rule that only binds the rival
wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for a card that makes players spend two animals a bid while it is out. `pledgeLadderDelta` does exactly that, and it does it to both Mayors — including the one who hired him — because a `displayed` city rule is a rule of the room, not of a town.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Split across the same card: the ladder is heavier while Faustus sits in the Capital City, and once a Mayor buys him out of the room they get the first bid of each turn a rung higher instead. Buying him is buying the door, which is the shape Bob's gate already established.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `opponentPledgeLadderPlus1`, a passive that raises the OTHER Mayor's pledge ladder and not its owner's, alongside the Statue burdens that already reach across the table. The Threadmaster keeps the displayed rule, which is a rule of the room and falls on everybody in it; buying him out of the display turns it into a rule that falls on your rival alone. Buying him is still buying the door — it is simply narrow on the other side of you now.

characters.name: Finn
characters.backstory:
Finn sells. Over the years he has sold hedge cuttings, subscriptions to a newspaper that was never printed, six identical clocks to the same household across four years, and — currently, legitimately, and rather well — most of the borough's dry goods. He is not a crook and he is not a saint, and the First Boroughs have known exactly where he sits on that line since he was about nine.

Clean jobs he has had plenty of. Weighing at the Grain Exchange, a season on the toll gate, two separate stints on the fair committee. They never last. Something always comes up that Finn cannot resist being clever about, and he moves on before anybody has to make it a formal matter, and everyone stays on speaking terms. What he has instead of a record is a reputation: if you need a thing sold, bought or valued inside the hour you go to Finn, you go in with your eyes open, and it gets done.

The odd part, which the borough long ago stopped finding odd, is that he is genuinely respected.
