He is on the committee more often than not, he chairs the fair, and when the Capital City sends somebody out to do business with the First Boroughs it is Finn who meets them, because he is the only animal in town who enjoys it. He keeps the fair's weights honest and he remembers, vividly, what the Finn of five years ago would have done with them.
characters.voice: Fast, friendly, already agreeing with you. Says 'look' a lot, and 'I'll be straight with you' — and is, about eighty per cent of the time.
characters.arc: All four rungs are the auction, because that is where Finn lives and it is what the maker asked for. Auctioneer's Boy (0) can only shout a number up. Peddler (1) puts a coin on his own announcement and sees what is coming next. Fair Warden (3) is the clean job: two Supply onto an auction he is already winning, and a tie breaks his way, because the animal calling the fair is the animal who knows the rules. Trade Broker (4) takes his percentage off everything the town brings home and reads the deck on the way in. He is a Fox the whole way: he never out-earns anybody, he wins the room.

characters.name: Fox Cub
characters.backstory:
Fox Cubs are not allowed inside the Auction House and every one of them knows what the big lots went for. They sit on the steps, they watch the animals coming out, and they read the faces — and a Fox Cub who has read the faces wrong twice does not read them wrong a third time.

As work they are nearly useless: three days of a Fox Cub buys the borough one Supply and a great deal of commentary. As an education it is the only one the species has ever needed. Nothing in the Auction House is taught. It is watched from the steps until it is obvious, which is why the ward counts the steps at two and the Auction House has never once objected.
characters.voice: Running commentary, pitched just loud enough to be overheard.
characters.arc: A Fox Cub counts for two when a Fox is set over them: the steps outside the room are half of what is ever taught about the room.

wantedArt.want: Fox Cub: A Cub on the steps called the timber lot four rungs before the room did, to nobody, and has been insufferable ever since.

characters.name: Fred
characters.backstory:
Fred is a mess, and the borough long ago stopped being surprised by it. He has been in Faustus's front window as an unbooked mannequin, up a ladder for Benjamin on a job nobody remembers hiring him for, and once, memorably, near the Bandstand on the Festival Green during a speech nobody has ever actually given from it — he says he was looking for the toilets, and the borough has decided to believe him, mostly because the alternatives are worse.

He is an Owl, so none of this happens by daylight, which is the only reason it has not cost him more than it has: whatever he has broken, wandered into, or been handed by an animal who barely knows his name gets sorted out well before the square wakes up to see it. He has held tools for Moss, held a ladder wrong for Benjamin, and been backstage crew for exactly one show he was never told the name of.

Nobody has worked out whether Fred is unlucky or whether he simply says yes to things, and Fred has never been asked in a way he could actually answer. What the whole borough agrees on is that when Fred is involved, something is going to happen, and it could go either way — which is why Roger, who chairs everything and decides nothing, has twice asked Fred to be the one who calls the ha'penny in the air, and been refused both times on the grounds that even that felt like too much responsibility.
characters.voice: Apologetic, easily distracted, and weirdly calm about disaster. Narrates his own bad luck like weather.
characters.arc: Every Fred carries the same shrug at a different price: toss a coin, and something changes for somebody — it is never fixed which side of the table it lands on.

wantedArt.why: No painted tile shows an animal roped into somebody else's job. All four borrow the Night Workers scene until one is commissioned.

characters.name: Gabe
characters.backstory:
The Salvage Yard is divided without anybody having said so: Annabelle takes the paper and Patch takes everything else. Gabe takes the third pile, which is what Patch has looked at and put down — a split glove, a bent spoon, half a curtain ring, the sort of thing even the yard has given up on — and out of it he makes a cast.

He has about forty of them now and they all have names. The shows are free and there are three regular ones: Saturday mornings in the Lending Library's children's corner, which is the slot Inkwell and Lynnette do not use; the bakery queue on the mornings Marmalade is handing out to the kittens first, which is a captive audience and Marmalade has never objected; and whatever room Cassadee will give him, late, when the list has run short. The children's version and the late version are not the same show and the borough has noticed.

Patch judges things for a living — animals bring him a thing and ask whether it is worth keeping, and then they start bringing him leases and seasons that have not gone well, and he is right. He has never once judged the third pile. Gabe is not his brother; Pockets is. But Gabe turns up at the yard about as often, is fed, and leaves with something, and Patch has never asked what for either.
characters.voice: Two voices, and neither of them his. Says almost nothing as himself and will not be drawn on which of the puppets he agrees with.
characters.arc: Raccoons work the bins, so Gabe's rungs go deeper into them. Corner Show (0) turns a card over. Puppet Maker (2) takes what the Capital City threw away — the Raccoon signature, doing exactly what the story says he does with it. Company of One (4) gets an Event back out of his own Town Dump, because the late show is the same script every time and he has never written it down. The Whole Cast (5) does both, every turn, which is forty puppets and one raccoon.

wantedArt.why: No painted tile shows a puppet booth. The Scrap Yard scene stands under the Puppet Maker and is exactly right there; the three show cards want a booth, a raccoon behind it, and a floor of kittens.

characters.name: Gwen
characters.backstory:
Gwen's diner is on the square, at the Hiring Hall corner, directly opposite Bean's café, and the two counters have divided the borough's bad mornings between them without ever discussing it. At Bean's you find out there is nothing on the board. At Gwen's you get a shift anyway.

That is the whole of her policy and she has never dressed it up. Anybody who walks in and asks for work gets an apron, that day, with no questions about why they are not doing whatever it is the borough thinks they do; there is no term, no interview and no mention of it afterwards. She pays at the end of the shift, in coin, and if you come back the next day she puts you on again, and if you never come back she does not ask Ned to write it down. The Hiring Hall has twice tried to make this a formal arrangement and twice been told, politely and at speed, that a formal arrangement would ruin it.

Rosabeth's gate takes the animals who have stopped getting up and Quill's orchard takes everybody, all the time, so that nobody has to admit to anything. Gwen's is the third of those doors and the least sentimental: the diner is busy, the griddle is hot, and there is no time to feel anything about it until the rush is over. Half the borough has worked a fortnight there between one career and the next, and the borough has agreed without agreeing anything that a fortnight at Gwen's is not worth mentioning.
characters.voice: Flat, fast and entirely unsentimental. Says 'apron's on the hook' rather than yes, and never says the other thing at all.
characters.arc: The rungs are about who counts as one of hers. Short-Order Cook (1) feeds one animal back onto the floor; Diner Keeper (3) puts anybody who works in Food back on the books cheap; Owner of the Diner (5) does it for anybody at all, whatever they think their job is, and still has the Food chit at the end of the shift. All three read out of the same policy, which is that a counter with a gap in it is a problem and an animal out of work is a solution.

wantedVerbs.why: The diner's actual rule is that anybody who walks in gets a shift, including an animal who is nobody's — out of the City Dump, or out of the other Mayor's Unemployment. Every rehiring verb in the engine reads your own Unemployment only.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Her rungs rehire and feed out of her own town's Unemployment, widening the filter as the cost climbs: Food only at 3, anybody at 5.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `rehireFromAnywhere` reads three queues rather than one — your own Unemployment, the rival's, and the hired help lying in the City Dump with no town to go back to — and `from` says which of them a given card may reach. An animal taken off the rival's books changes hands rather than being copied, which is why the card census counts deck cards across both towns instead of one at a time. Gwen has two cards for it: Anybody's Counter reads her own books and the Dump, and The Apron on the Hook reads all three.

wantedArt.why: No painted tile shows a diner counter mid-rush. The three cards stand on the Community Kitchen scene, which is the right warmth and the wrong room — Gwen's is a griddle, a hatch, a row of stools and an apron on a hook by the door.

characters.name: Harrison
characters.backstory:
Harrison is the Fox on the piano in Oatmeal's band, and the Fox on the piano in everybody else's. He cannot read a note, has never learned, and can follow an animal who has never rehearsed anything in their life through a song he has not heard — eight bars in he has the shape of it, and by the second verse he is a half-step ahead, putting the chord under the note the singer is about to reach for.

That is the whole of his talent and it is not really a musical one: Harrison knows what a room is going to want before the room does. Cassadee books him without asking who else is on. Finn, who meets the Capital City's traders because he is the only animal in town who enjoys it, has twice taken Harrison along to sit at the back of a negotiation and say nothing, and both times has come home with the number he wanted. Harrison will not discuss this and puts it down to the piano.

Lynnette printed a paragraph about him once, in the paper, about an animal who plays for four hours a week and cannot read a word of it. Harrison has never mentioned the paragraph and has never had it framed, and it is on the wall at the back of the open mic room where he cannot see it from the stool.
characters.voice: Amiable, unhurried, and a half-step ahead of you. Answers the question you are about to ask.
characters.arc: Foxes read the room, so Harrison reads the Capital City. Piano Boy (0) glances at what is coming; House Pianist (2) puts the top of the deck back in the order he wants it; Band Leader (4) does both at once and makes the next raise cheaper, which is the same trick applied to a room full of bidders.

wantedArt.why: The Bandstand is the right borough and the wrong instrument: it holds a band of five if two stand on the step, and Harrison is one fox and an upright piano in a room with the chairs pushed back.

characters.name: Hazel
characters.backstory:
Hazel keeps raccoon hours, which in the First Boroughs means the useful ones. The stall goes up when the lamps go on and comes down somewhere around four, and everything on it is interesting: bottles with no labels, a drawer of keys to doors nobody can place, charts of a sky that is not quite this one, and — reliably, unpredictably — the one thing you needed and could not have named. Where any of it comes from is Hazel's business. They work the bins, the barges and the City Dump, and they get there first.

They are, by common agreement, a bit much. They read the cards, they read the sky, they will tell you what the month means and then tell you the price, and they are never entirely joking. Half the borough takes the mysticism as part of the patter. The other half has quietly noticed how often Hazel turns out to be right about what is coming up for sale.

None of which has stopped the town putting them in charge of things. Hazel has run the guild hall twice, has sat on the market committee for years, and is who the night trade sends when it wants to be heard in daylight. They arrive at the meeting in the coat they closed the stall in, say one useful thing, and go to bed at eight in the morning.
characters.voice: Amused, sideways, fond of a pause. Gives you the price and then something you did not ask for that turns out to matter.
characters.arc: Every rung gets a card out of the deck and into a paw, which is what the maker asked for. Barrow Hand (0) draws off her own slow shift. Night Market Vendor (1) draws and bins on arrival. Market Vendor (2) sets the top of the deck in order, which is the reading before the selling. Guildmaster (3) is the Raccoon signature: the City Dump is stock, and the guild hall is where it finally gets sold in daylight. Merchant (5) turns every card the town brings home into another card in hand, and bins what the deck was going to waste your draw on. Hazel's Night Market is the same instinct as an Event — take the good half off the top. Added since: a Market Committee Chair at 4 who draws every turn there is another Raccoon in the town — the night trade's voice at a daylight meeting.

characters.name: Hibiscus
characters.backstory:
Hibiscus walks the borough's round. Juniper takes the post that leaves the borough and Hibiscus takes the post that stays in it, and the two of them hand over at the sorting bench every morning at five, which is the only part of the day Hibiscus does quickly. After that it is doors. Every door, in order, and at a fair number of them somebody comes out, and that is where the schedule goes.

They are not bad at the job. They are, by any measure the Hiring Hall keeps, extremely good at it: nothing is lost, nothing is misdelivered, and Hibiscus knows which house on which lane has somebody in it who has not been seen for three days, which is a thing no ledger in the borough records. It is simply that a round which ought to take four hours takes seven, because a bunny who genuinely wants to know how your mother is cannot be got off a doorstep in under ten minutes, and they genuinely want to know, at every door, every day. The borough has decided this is the arrangement. Complaints about the late second post are filed at the Hiring Hall next to the ones about the county gate and come to about as much.

What the round actually does is get the borough up. Hibiscus arrives, the door opens, somebody who was going to have a slow morning is now standing in it with their apron on and an opinion about the ferry, and by the time the round is done half the lane is out of doors and working. Biff walks his beat to stop trouble. Hibiscus walks theirs and the trouble never starts, which nobody has ever put in a report.
characters.voice: Bright, unhurried, endlessly interested. Opens with a question about somebody's family and gets the answer. Says 'no, go on' at the exact moment they should be leaving.
characters.arc: Five rungs of the same round, waking more of the town each time. The Post Runner at 1 gets one animal up for the morning. The Night Mail at 2 does it on the way home as well. The Round Walker at 3 turns a finished shift into somebody else's start. The Mail Coach Driver at 4 keeps the hour whether the passengers are aboard or not — the one job where Hibiscus is early — and has somebody up and waiting the moment the town announces anything. The Postmaster at 5 is the whole lane out of doors by nine: Hibiscus comes up, and an animal who was going to have a slow morning is standing in the doorway with their apron on.

characters.name: Hoglet
characters.backstory:
Hoglets are put on the gate step, which is the safest place in the borough and also the one where you learn the most. Everybody comes past the gate. A Hoglet who has spent a season on the step knows every animal's name, their business, and which of them tells the gate a different story on the way back.

They are slow to give the borough anything — three days for a Supply, and the step is not paid work — and they are also, from the first week, completely immovable about who is allowed past. Bristle says that is not something you teach. Bristle says you either come out of the nest with it or you do not, which is also why the ward has never counted the step as much of an apprenticeship: there was nothing to learn, so there is nothing to credit.
characters.voice: Polite, unhurried, and entirely unbudgeable.
characters.arc: A season on the gate step is where a Hedgehog learns the only thing Hedgehogs teach, and any Hedgehog in the borough may be played over a Hoglet afterwards.

wantedArt.want: Hoglet: Bristle let one hold the gate for an afternoon as a joke. Two carters and a Fox turned round and came back with their paperwork.

characters.name: Hoot
characters.backstory:
Hoot came in on the night mail with one bag and a list of everybody's names, and had worked through most of the list by the end of the first week. The job is night porter: doors, lamps, deliveries, the ward's keys, and getting animals up who have asked to be got up. The knocking at four in the morning is neither a joke nor an accident — Hoot takes a request to be woken as seriously as anybody in the First Boroughs takes anything, and has never once been late with one.

Nobody has worked out yet when Hoot sleeps. They are new enough that the borough still says so, and settled enough that nobody can remember the last week without them.

The kitchen came later and came the same way the list did: nobody asked for it. If you are going to knock on a door at four in the morning you had better have something with you, so Hoot started carrying something, and then started making it, and the ward's night kitchen is now a room with a bell on it and a rota. The list of everybody's names has what they take in the morning written beside it, and Hoot has never once had to look.
characters.voice: Bright, polite, appallingly awake. Apologises for the hour, and then knocks again.
characters.arc: The porter's round and the night kitchen are the same round: doors, lamps, keys, and now breakfast. The dear versions wake the whole town before dawn and feed it.

wantedArt.want: Hoot's new versions.

characters.name: Inkwell
characters.backstory:
Inkwell reads the sky the way other animals read the paper, and tells the rest of it back as stories. By day — what there is of day, for a cat keeping the hours Inkwell keeps — they are in the library with the star charts out and four books open at once, working on something they will explain at length to anybody who asks and which nobody has ever entirely followed. By night they are on the Observatory steps with a flask, looking up.

The children get the good version. Every week, in the corner of the Lending Library, Inkwell tells the little ones about the worlds on the other side of ours: the doors in the hedge, the town under the lake, the cousins of the moon and what they are like. The stories have a geography and they never contradict one another, which is more than can be said for most of the borough's history. Inkwell insists, cheerfully, that it is all research.

There is a long-standing rumour that Inkwell is a mage, and Inkwell has never once denied it, which is exactly the sort of thing Inkwell would do. What is true is that things go slightly still around them. The reading room goes quiet, the clock in the hall seems to take its time, and animals who meant to leave an hour ago find that they have not. Cats do as they please, and what pleases Inkwell is for the evening to go on a little longer.
characters.voice: Unhurried, delighted, permanently mid-thought. Begins answers with 'well — that depends which sky you mean'.
characters.arc: Lore is the storytelling and Science is the looking. Bookmark Keeper (1) hands the whole town an extra step of morning. Storyteller (2) has one animal back on their feet by the next turn because the story ended well. Night Librarian (3) is the stillness itself: nobody's animals advance at the next Ready, yours included — the evening simply does not end. Astronomer (4) reads the Capital City's deck off the shift, reads the rival's hand in the same breath, and once in a game gets up when a cat should not be able to: the Cat signature and the whole rumour in one card. Keeper of Stories (5) turns the first Lore Event of every turn into a card and an extra step. The two Events are the two halves of them: the late shift with the children, and the chart drawn from the good chair.

wantedVerbs.verb: peekOpponentHand / a 'the other side of the glass' effect
wantedVerbs.why: The mage rumour wanted one card that looks somewhere no other card looks — the rival's hand, or the Capital City's Ordinance display — as the thing nobody can prove Inkwell does.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Kept the looking inside the vocabulary: `peekMarketDeck` off the Astronomer's shift, and `blockNextReady` for the stillness. The rumour stays in the flavor, where it belongs.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `peekOpponentHand`: the one effect in the collection that looks into a rival's hand. It moves nothing and it is not secret — the rival is told they were read, because a card that looked without saying so would be a card nobody could play around. The Astronomer reads the Market Deck and the hand off the same shift, which is the rumour said out loud at last.

characters.name: JT
characters.backstory:
JT is a nurse and he is very silly, and the borough worked out years ago that those are the same fact. The children's ward is his — he took it, nobody assigned it — and he takes it seriously enough to have a bit for every procedure in it, most of them terrible, all of them load-bearing. An animal who is laughing is an animal who is not bracing, and an animal who is not bracing is half a minute's work instead of ten.

He works under Shay and ahead of her, in the way good nurses do: the small animals, the cheap hours, the ones who have not got a Supply to their name and turn up anyway. Nobody in the First Boroughs has put more animals back on their feet for less.

Three evenings a week he is at the restaurant in a clean shirt doing the juice list, which is not a joke and is not a hobby. He can tell you what the pears were doing that summer. He runs the pairing for the Auction House's big lots, he has opinions about pressing that he will share at length, and he has never once let a child at the next table be served anything less interesting than what the adults are drinking.
characters.voice: Two voices: the one with the funny hat on, and the one that says 'now, the pears'.
characters.arc: The cheap JTs are the ward — a Supply saved, an apprentice back on their feet. The dear ones are the restaurant, and the restaurant only ever pours for the animals at the top of the bill.

wantedArt.want: Every version of JT.

characters.name: Jake
characters.backstory:
Jake came out from the Capital City with a reputation the Hiring Hall has never been given the details of, and has never asked for, because the one time somebody did ask he told them and they wished they had not. He is a warren runner: the long errands, the far rows, the sacks at the wrong end of the borough at the wrong end of the night. It is the job nobody wants and he is frankly wasted in it, and both of those things are the point.

He is down on his luck in the specific, cheerful way of an animal who has been down on his luck before and knows exactly how long it lasts. He does not borrow. He does not explain. He turns up at the grange, says what he will do it for, does about three animals' worth of it, takes the money in his paw rather than on the book, and then one morning the borough looks round and Jake is not there. He has done it twice. Nobody has an address for him. The road is the point — he talks about it the way Benjamin talks about light, which is to say constantly and without embarrassment.

The borough's older animals compare him to Kevin, and the comparison is wrong in the way that matters. Kevin stays a fortnight and every one of his eleven employers would have him back. Jake leaves before anybody has decided anything about him at all, which is a trick, and which is the same trick every time.
characters.voice: Quick, funny, slightly too familiar on the first morning. Never answers a question about where he was. Says "before I go" a lot, from the first day.
characters.arc: One rung, and it is a short one on purpose. Jake is hired out of the Capital City, works like three animals for two turns, and is on the road — the whole of him is the trade between what he earns you and how little of him you get to keep.

wantedVerbs.verb: a hire who can be re-hired after leaving
wantedVerbs.why: Jake has done it twice and the story wants the borough to be able to take him on again the next time he drifts through. A `leavesAfter` hire goes back to the Capital City and the card is simply out of the game for that Mayor.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Two turns, a big shift, and the Supply in his paw. The second visit is a story the flavor tells rather than a thing the engine does.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `returnsToMarket` on a card with `leavesAfter`. When the retainer is up Jake goes to the bottom of the Market Deck instead of the City Dump, so the next time the deck comes round to him either Mayor may take him on again. The card now says what the story always said — he leaves, and he turns up again — and `power.js` pays it as the chance it is rather than as a second term.

characters.name: Jessica
characters.backstory:
Jessica teaches the little ones, and she has never in her life set homework. The borough's parents raised this with her once, some years ago, in a meeting; Jessica agreed that homework was a very good idea and said she would think about it, and then went back and taught them the constellations as a round with actions. The kittens can name every one of them. Not one of them can spell any of them. The parents have stopped bringing it up.

The method is songs, games and activities, in that order, and it is not a softness — it is the only thing she has ever found that works on an animal who is convinced they are no good at this. She gets them singing the thing before they know it is the thing. By the time a kitten notices they are doing arithmetic they have been doing it for a fortnight and are annoyed about having been tricked, which Jessica regards as the moment the job is done.

She runs the night school as well, which is where the other half of her work happens, because the animals who turn up at the night school are not kittens. They are animals already doing a job who have worked out they would like to be doing a better one, and Jessica is the one who finds the next rung and talks them onto it before they have finished explaining why they could not possibly. Half the Hiring Hall's promotions in the last ten years started in that room. She is small, extremely loud, and has never once been to bed before four.
characters.voice: Delighted, fast, and slightly out of breath. Everything is an activity. Ends explanations with "— right, everybody up".
characters.arc: Four rungs and no homework. The Song and Game Leader at 0 is the Owl signature done literally: everybody up, on their feet, now. The Infant Teacher at 1 and the Night School Teacher at 2 start paying for the next rung — a promotion in your own town costs less. The Headmistress at 4 hands that rate out every morning, at double, which is what ten years of the night school actually amounts to.

wantedArt.why: The songs-and-games rung is a room of kittens on their feet doing the constellations as a round with actions. It carries nightworkers/3, the Headmistress at her desk, as a stand-in, which is the one thing Jessica is never doing.

characters.name: Juniper
characters.backstory:
Juniper carries the post, and has since they were small: the borough's letters, the grange's notices, the Capital City's forms, up and down the same routes in every weather there is. What makes them good at it was never the legs. It is that Juniper can put a thing to an animal in the way that animal needs to hear it, which is a rarer skill than the town knew it was short of, and it has carried them from a satchel to the ward office to the committee table without anybody quite planning it. They are, at time of writing, on four committees and chair two of them.

None of that is what Juniper is actually about. Juniper reads the sky. They keep an ephemeris, they know which planet is where and what the almanac says about it, and when a decision comes down to a genuinely even choice they will go outside, look up, and come back with an answer. The Science hall finds this maddening and the Observatory finds it charming, and both have had to admit that Juniper's calls come off more often than they have any business doing.

Ask them and they will tell you there is no conflict in it at all. The post goes where it is addressed and the stars say when to set out; one is the route and the other is the hour. Juniper has never missed a delivery, and has never made a decision on a cloudy night without complaining about it first.
characters.voice: Warm, quick, disarming. Delivers bad news kindly and then tells you what the sky is doing.
characters.arc: Civics is the ladder and the auction is the Fox. Messenger (1) reads the Capital City's deck on every announcement, because knowing what is coming is the job. Courier Captain (2) makes the first bid of your turn count for more. Ward Councillor (3) puts two Supply onto an auction they are already winning. Diplomat (4) stops the rival raising at all, which is the committee room in one sentence. Stargazer (5) leaves the ladder alone entirely and looks at the deck at the start of every turn — and with another Science animal in town, the sky pays. The rise through Civics is the trade; the Science card at the top is what Juniper would have done with the whole life if the post had let them.

characters.name: Kevin
characters.backstory:
Kevin came out from the Capital City at seventeen because somebody told him there was work, and there was. He is the easiest hire in the First Boroughs: he says yes before you have finished the sentence, he is at the yard before the animal who hired him, and for about a fortnight he is worth two of anybody. Then the fortnight ends. Kevin goes flat all at once, sleeps through a morning, apologises far more than anyone wants him to, and is on to the next thing by the end of the week.

The borough has worked out how to use him and mostly does not mind. You get Kevin for a short stretch, you get a great deal out of it, and you do not build anything long around him. He is nineteen and has had eleven jobs, and every one of them would have him back.

What he does with the flat fortnight is read. Novels, four or five on the go at once, in stacks by the bed and the kettle and the chair and one on the windowsill of whatever room he is renting that month. Lynnette keeps him a shelf at the print shop. He will tell you the plots of all five at once, badly, with enormous enthusiasm, and then he is up and off again.
characters.voice: Eager, loud, slightly out of breath. Says 'yeah — yeah, no, I can do that', and means it, right up until he cannot.
characters.arc: One card, hired out of the Capital City and built the way the maker described him. He arrives with money in his paw and works flat out for three Supply — then two, then one, because that is how Kevin works and always has — throws Supply onto an auction you are winning, and after three of your turns he is gone back to the city. Get the first shift out of him; that is the one you are paying for.

wantedVerbs.verb: burnout (a shift that degrades, or a Character who unemploys himself)
wantedVerbs.why: 'Burns himself out easily' wanted the output to fall off across his stay — three, then two, then one — or for Kevin to put himself into Unemployment at the end of it.
wantedVerbs.workaround: `leavesAfter` does the honest half of it: the gains stay quick and the stay is short, and he is simply gone on the fourth turn. A falling shift output would need the engine to re-read a stack's shift each time it starts.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `shift.decay`: every shift a Character works pays `decay` less than the one before, down to `minOutput`. The count lives on the stack (`shiftsWorked`), so burning out is a property of the animal rather than of the card, and an animal who never works never burns out. Kevin is 3, then 2, then 1, which is the maker's sentence exactly; his term went to three turns so the whole fall is visible, and `power.js` rates a decaying shift on the average of the shifts it will actually work.

characters.name: Kitten
characters.backstory:
The night school's front row is Kittens, and Jessica has never set them any homework. They can name every constellation and cannot spell any of them, which is on the record in this borough as a complete success.

A Kitten will give you three days and one Supply, on a schedule of the Kitten's choosing, and will then be asleep somewhere warm and impossible to reach. Cats do as they please and they start as they mean to go on. Nobody has ever got a Kitten to co-operate with another Kitten and the Hiring Hall has stopped putting it on the board.
characters.voice: Wide awake at the wrong hour, and very pleased about it.
characters.arc: The first rung of every Cat's ladder — and any Cat in the borough may turn out to be the one who was standing there.

wantedArt.want: Kitten: Marmalade sends the front row home with buns. The buns do not reach the front row's homes and Marmalade has never asked about it.

characters.name: Lindsay
characters.backstory:
Lindsay is not paying attention. She has not been paying attention for about twenty years and the glasshouse has never been better. She waters along the bench with the can held out at exactly the right height for exactly the right count, eyes somewhere past the roof glass, thinking about something that has nothing whatever to do with the roof glass, and every pot gets what it wants. Ask her afterwards what she did and she cannot tell you. Ask the pots and they can.

What she is thinking about is never quite established. She has been overheard costing out a glasshouse on the moon, working out how far a seed could fall, and settling an argument nobody was having about whether rain has a smell before or after it lands. The borough finds this restful. Rosabeth sings to her plants in full view and has done for thirty years; Lindsay does the opposite and gets the same result, and between the two of them the borough has stopped expecting gardening to make sense. The one place it shows up as a problem is a conversation: she will agree warmly with something you did not say and then ask you a question you already answered.

Her beds come in over. Always, every year, more than the row should give, and she cannot account for it and has stopped trying — she says the counting is somebody else's department and she is right, it is Orien's, and his figures on her glasshouse have a note in the margin that just says 'ask her again in spring'. Marmalade gets her rosemary and will not use anybody else's. Comet, who has been turned down twice by a selection board for wanting the moon too openly, likes her enormously.
characters.voice: Dreamy, kind, half a beat late. Trails off mid-sentence and comes back to it four minutes later, correctly. Says 'oh — sorry — yes' more than any other animal in the borough.
characters.arc: Five rungs of not paying attention, paying better and better. The Potting Helper at 0 finishes a shift and comes up with more than the row should give. The Glasshouse Hand at 2 keeps the whole growing side earning while there is another Agriculture animal about. The Herb Grower at 3 is the daydream itself: she is halfway through something else and does the work anyway, because it is second nature — the one time a Cat's own rules do not apply to her. The Conservatory Keeper at 4 has the benches producing over for everybody. The Moon Gardener at 5 is where her head has been the whole time, and the borough finally gets paid for it.

characters.name: Liz
characters.backstory:
Liz keeps the weighbridge at the Grain Exchange. Every loaded cart in or out of the borough's biggest building crosses her plate, and what she writes on the docket is what everybody after her is paid on. Copper's office certifies the bridge every spring and has never once had to adjust it.

It is the job Finn had and lost, which the borough mentions to neither of them. Liz is a Fox and reads a carter's face while the beam is settling, and has never needed to do anything about what she reads there, because the beam settles where it settles.
characters.voice: Short, level, faintly bored. Reads the number out once.
characters.arc: Scale Hand (1) is the beam and somebody else's docket; Weighbridge Keeper (4) is the beam, the docket and the signature. A weighbridge does not need an ability: the whole of its power is that the number is the number.

wantedArt.why: Liz is a new animal and no painted tile shows this job. With no `art` set the cards fall back to the painted Fox scene, which is the right species doing the wrong work.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_liz_scale_hand_1 → the makerharvest atlas, tile 10; mk_liz_weighbridge_keeper_4 → the makerharvest atlas, tile 11. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Liza
characters.backstory:
Liza is on Cassadee's list more often than anybody except Oatmeal's band, and unlike the band she comes on her own, with nothing, and sings for twenty minutes to a room that stops moving. She has done this since she was seventeen. She has never been paid more than the hat, has never asked to be, and has turned down the Festival Green twice on the grounds that it is too big a room to be honest in.

The borough gossips about one thing where that room is concerned, very quietly, and Liza is one half of it and does not know. Thistle comes on the nights she is on the list, stands at the back by the door, does not take his coat off, listens to the one set with his eyes shut and is gone before the applause; Cassadee has twice moved Liza up the running order so that he would not have to stay so late, and has never mentioned it to either of them.

Between bookings Liza works Gwen's counter, which is the least remarkable fact about her and the one she would give you first. She is quick on a hatch, she remembers an order without writing it down, and she sings while she does it, which Gwen permits on the grounds that the rush goes faster.
characters.voice: Offhand about everything except the running order. Talks about her own singing the way other animals talk about the weather in a week they were not there for.
characters.arc: Rabbits fill rooms, so Liza's rungs fill a town. Floor Singer (0) is twenty minutes and a hat. Counter Singer (1) is the fortnight at Gwen's and pays like it. Top of the Bill (3) gets somebody else in the town back on their feet, and Headliner (5) brings a whole other animal in out of hand, which is what a room that is suddenly full actually looks like from the door.

wantedArt.why: The Open Mic Night scene is the right room and shows no singer in it. A rabbit alone at the front of a stopped room, hat on the floor, is the painting these three want.

characters.name: Lynnette
characters.backstory:
Lynnette prints the town's books. The press is hers, the shop is hers, and the borough's paper, ballots, almanacs, hymn sheets, notices and every book printed in the First Boroughs these fifteen years have come off it — usually late, always right. She got the press cheap because it was broken and learned to mend it because nobody else would, which is roughly her whole biography: a thing needed doing, and doing it turned out to be a trade.

What she actually loves is the spreading. Lynnette cannot leave a good thing unpublished. If an animal in the borough learns something worth knowing she will have it set, printed and pinned up in the Hiring Hall inside the week, free, whether or not they asked — the apprentice notices, the guild's syllabus and the almanac's planting tables are all her doing and not one of them ever made her a penny. She is the reason an animal in the First Boroughs can find out how to be better at their job without knowing anybody first.

Thursdays she reads to the little ones in the Lending Library, sitting on the floor with about nine rabbits and whoever else has wandered in, doing all the voices. She is a poor businesswoman and a rich one in the way the borough actually counts it.
characters.voice: Brisk, ink to the elbows, always mid-job. Finishes your sentence, and then prints it.
characters.arc: Every rung makes the next animal easier to take on, and the step up cheaper than the new body — which is what the maker asked for. Night Printer (0) takes a coin off your next recruit the moment she arrives, and two off it if it is somebody you already have going up a rung. Bookbinder (1) does the same off every shift she works. Lending Librarian (3) is the Rabbit signature — she reads to them, and one of them walks out of your hand into the town behind her. Master Printer (5) is the point of all of it: your Masters are ready a turn sooner, because by the time they turn up the borough has already read how the job is done. Added since: a Press Feeder at 2 with no ability — the night's run itself, which discounts nothing and produces everything.

wantedVerbs.verb: upgradeDiscount (a recruit discount that only applies to a higher version of a Character already in your town)
wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for abilities that help characters upgrade. Upgrading is recruiting a dearer version over a cheaper one, but `recruitDiscount` cannot tell that recruit from any other — the mod's `filter` reads study, species and cost, not 'this card upgrades one of yours'.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Left the discount untyped, so it helps any recruit and helps an upgrade among them, and put the real answer on the Master Printer: `masterDelayMinus1`, which makes the top of every character's arc a turn cheaper in time. A filter key like `upgradesOwn` would let the Night Printer and the Bookbinder say it exactly.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as a mod filter key, `upgradesOwn`. Whether a recruit is an upgrade is not a property of the card — the same card is a promotion or a new body depending on who is standing in the town — so `recruitCost` passes it in and `modFilterMatches` reads it there. The Night Printer and the Bookbinder now each hand out two discounts, the plain one and the printer's rate, and only an upgrade collects both.

characters.name: Mandee
characters.backstory:
Mandee works nights. Only nights — the courier run, the weather watch on the dome, the trestles coming down at Hazel's market at four, the loads that go on the water when the water is empty. She is at the sorting bench before Hibiscus and gone before Juniper, she is on Taco's cart list, and she has never once been seen in the First Boroughs in daylight by an animal who could later produce a witness.

Nobody knows where she lives. This is not a figure of speech and the borough has tested it: Hoot keeps the list of animals who have asked to be woken and Mandee is not on it, the Hiring Hall has a line for an address and hers is blank, and twice now somebody has set out to walk with her at the end of a run and found, perfectly pleasantly, that they were walking home alone. The borough has two animals it does not ask about — Barnaby is the other — and has decided not to compare notes, which is itself a decision it made without discussing.

What she trades in, besides freight, is tales. They are very good tales. They are about the far bank and the long road and a thing at the county line in a bad winter, they are told at exactly the pace of a walk, and not one of them has ever been checked. Scott, who has Ned certify everything he prints about a real animal or a real year, keeps a whole shelf of Mandee's and files it with the invention, and has said, once, in a way that was not a joke, that he is not sure that is the right shelf.

And she is never slow. Whatever she is hired to be — the courier, the watcher, the trader with the good coat — Mandee arrives on her feet and ready to go, at an hour when everybody else is turning over.
characters.voice: Low, amused, unhurried. Answers a question with a story that is almost an answer. Says "I'll be off, then" while already off.
characters.arc: Four rungs and no daylight. The Night Courier at 1 is a Fox reading the Capital City one card ahead. From the Weather Watcher at 2 upward, every rung carries the same line — recruit, and somebody turns one step toward upright, and the animal she picks is usually herself, which is the promise the maker made about her. The Moonlight Trader at 3 adds the Fox's first bid; the Keeper of Tales at 4 makes the whole town's Masters arrive a turn nearer, which is Mandee's own habit finally spreading to everybody else.

wantedVerbs.verb: entersUpright (a card that sets its own entry orientation)
wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for all of Mandee's variations to arrive ready, regardless of class. Entry orientation is read off the cost alone (`entryOrientation` in actions.js) before the animal is even on the table, so a card cannot change its own — the only two things that touch it, `masterDelayMinus1` and the Statue of Patience's burden, are player passives already in force when the recruit happens.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Three of them: an Apprentice rung, which arrives upright by the rules anyway; `onRecruit → advanceCharacter` on every rung above it, which the player spends on Mandee herself to stand her up the moment she lands; and `masterDelayMinus1` on the Keeper of Tales, so the next Master this town hires — Mandee included — comes in a turn nearer. An upgrade recruit keeps the stack's orientation, so once one Mandee is upright the rest of her arc genuinely does arrive ready. `advanceCharacter` is the Owl's signature and this is the one place a Fox borrows it; she keeps `peekMarketDeck` and `firstBidPlus1` so the auction animal is still the animal.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `entersUpright` on a card. Entry orientation is otherwise read off the cost alone, before the animal is on the table; this is the one thing that can say otherwise, and it is read by the recruit action and by `recruitFromHand` alike, so she arrives ready however she got here. All four Mandees carry it. The Statue of Patience's burden still sits her down, because that is a rule of the town and this is only a fact about one animal — and the `onRecruit → advanceCharacter` workaround has come off the rungs that only had it to stand her up.

characters.name: Maribel
characters.backstory:
Maribel has been a tree hugger since she was small enough to be carried past the hedgerow, and she means it literally: the oak on the far side of the allotment strip is standing today because a six-year-old mouse sat in the roots of it for a day and a half while the grange argued overhead. She has never really stopped doing that, she has only got better at the paperwork.

The seed bank is the grown-up version of the oak. Maribel keeps it — every variety the borough has ever grown, dried, labelled, doubled and put away against the year somebody needs it, and the labels are hers because she does not trust anybody else's. She is the animal who reads the whole ordinance before the meeting, finds the clause that saves the hedgerow, and files the objection again on the Monday after it is thrown out on the Friday. Clover's allotment strip has four generations behind it and Maribel has the seed stock for all four in a tin.

What she is bad at is the Capital City. She does not bid, she does not enjoy being outbid, and a borough busy raising Buildings is a borough turning ground she has walked over since she was a kit into something that cannot be turned back. She would rather the town grew slowly and kept what it has, and she will say so, at length, in writing, on the record.
characters.voice: Patient, precise, faintly damp. Says 'that hedge is older than the bylaw' and has the date for both.
characters.arc: Maribel is the Mouse who makes the town's paperwork cheap, and every rung makes it cheaper. The Seed Keeper (1) takes a Character off the next Event. The Seed Bank Clerk (2) starts pulling Events back out of the Town Dump — nothing filed is ever really thrown away. The Seed Vault Scientist (3) is paid in cards for the Science the borough asks her for. The Horticulturist (4) pays for every Event, and pays extra while the ground is still ground. The Seed Bank Director (5) is the objection standing as a rule: an Event every single turn needs one animal fewer, which is what a lifetime of filing on the Monday actually buys. Added since: a Seed Sorter at 0 with no ability — trays and tweezers, before there was a vault to make cheap.

characters.name: Marmalade
characters.backstory:
Marmalade was a horrible kitten. He shoved, he took things, he was walked home by Biff more times than anyone has the heart to count, and the borough had more or less decided what he was going to be. Then somebody put him in front of a bowl of dough to keep his paws busy, and he was quiet for the first time in his life.

Nothing about the anger has come back. It went into the proving and it stayed there. Marmalade bakes at night, because that is when the ovens are banked, and by morning he has been through three recipes nobody asked for — a loaf in the shape of a hedgehog, buns with the wrong fruit in on purpose, something laminated he read about and could not leave alone. Half of it is handed out before it is paid for, always to the kittens first, because Marmalade knows precisely what a kitten with nothing to do turns into.

He works the market stall in the day and cannot keep a queue moving to save his life, since everybody in it wants to tell him something. He is a Cat, so he does this entirely on his own schedule and is impossible to hurry; but the borough gets up earlier on the mornings Marmalade has been baking, and that is most of them.
characters.voice: Warm, distractible, covered in flour. Starts sentences with 'right, so listen' and ends them with a bun in your paw.
characters.arc: Every rung of Marmalade gets the town up and moving earlier, because that is what the bread does. The Night Baker (0) works the long patient shift and has everyone a step further along by the Ready. The Dough Kneader (1) and the Market Baker (2) do it at the door, the moment he is hired, and the Market Baker takes a coin at the counter for it. The Neighborhood Baker (3) hands the tray round and puts one of your animals back on its feet outright. The Harvest Head Baker (5) is the whole bakery: the first shift each turn pays extra, and once a game Marmalade is simply up before the rest of the town, which is the Cat's own trick and his oldest habit. Added since: an Oven Keeper at 4 who is paid every morning the town has another Cat in it — the kittens, served first, paying him back.

wantedVerbs.verb: giveToUnemployed (handing food to an animal out of work)
wantedVerbs.why: The story wants the buns to reach the animals with nothing — a Character in your Unemployment turning back up because Marmalade fed it.
wantedVerbs.workaround: The Neighborhood Baker readies a Character already in town instead: the same gesture, aimed at an animal who is at least standing. `rehire` is the Badger's verb and it costs Supply, which is exactly what Marmalade does not charge.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `giveToUnemployed`, and pointedly not a rehire: an animal in your own Unemployment is fed and turns back up Busy, and no Supply changes hands, so a rehire discount neither helps nor applies. The Neighborhood Baker hands the tray to whoever costs 2 or less — the kittens first, as the flavor always said.

characters.name: Mildred
characters.backstory:
Mildred has been behind the counter at the Counting House for longer than most of the borough has been alive, and she is slow. She is slow on purpose. The queue knows it, the queue has always known it, and the queue forms anyway, because in forty-one years Mildred has not made a single error and the ward records say so — Ned has checked, twice, unasked.

She is friendly and she is absolutely immovable about the rules. She will explain the rule. She will explain why the rule is the rule. She will tell you, kindly, what you could bring in tomorrow that would let her say yes. And then she will say no today, and she will say it to a Mayor exactly as she says it to anybody else, which is the single most expensive habit in the First Boroughs and the reason the borough's money has never once gone missing.

What a Mayor across the table notices is subtler and worse: while Mildred is on her feet, every shift in the other town seems to come up a little short. Nothing is taken. Nothing is refused. There is simply a form, and the form is correct, and the form takes a while.
characters.voice: Unhurried, courteous, and entirely final. 'I can do that for you tomorrow.'
characters.arc: The rungs are how far the counter reaches. The clerk keeps her own books; the Branch Manager keeps everybody's, and the other town feels it on every shift it finishes.

wantedArt.want: Every version of Mildred.

characters.name: Mimi
characters.backstory:
Mimi works the cabin, which is five jobs in a uniform designed to look like one. She is the safety demonstration and the trolley and the pressure check and the welcome at the front step and the animal who settles the bill at the far end, and she moves between all five so smoothly that most passengers come off the aircraft believing they have been looked after by one extremely calm rabbit and not by a small institution.

She flies with Reese most weeks. The sunglasses do not work on her. She has never told him so, which he has correctly identified as worse.

Nothing gets to her. A diverted landing, a broken trolley latch, a passenger who has strong feelings about the seat numbering — all of it gets the same unhurried smile and the same sentence, delivered while she is already fixing it. The single exception is on the record and the borough does not raise it: the flight they ran out of beets. Mimi was not unpleasant. Mimi was not anything. She simply went very quiet for forty minutes, and everyone aboard understood that something had happened that was not going to happen twice. We don't talk about that time.
characters.voice: Warm, level, already solving it. 'Of course — give me one moment.'
characters.arc: She does not climb; she changes hats, and the whole point of her is that the hat can change mid-shift and the post does not. The dear version is the one who is running the whole cabin and can still put another body out of the door with her.

wantedArt.want: Every version of Mimi.

characters.name: Mittens
characters.backstory:
Mittens is the rooftop cat. It is above you — on the Hiring Hall, on the long ridge over the night market, on the Observatory dome on a clear night — and it has been there for some time before you noticed. Nobody knows where it came from. The Hiring Hall has it on the books because somebody had to write something on the line, and what they wrote was 'Mittens', which is not information.

It watches. That is most of what it does, and the borough has stopped finding it strange, in the way it stopped finding Rosabeth's singing strange. But every so often, in a meeting that has gone round three times or a yard where two animals have been staring at a broken thing for an hour, Mittens says one sentence from somewhere above head height and the problem is over. Then it is not there any more.

The standing theory is that it is simply the only animal in the First Boroughs who sees the whole town at once, and that everything else follows from that. Nobody has tested the theory. You would have to find Mittens first.
characters.voice: One sentence, from above, at the exact moment it is needed. Never a second sentence.
characters.arc: One card, hired out of the Capital City as it always was, and the two halves of it are the two things Mittens does. It readies itself once a game, because a rooftop cat has never once been where it was supposed to be; and when it comes upright it puts the top of your deck in the order you wanted, because it has been up there looking at what is coming the whole time.

characters.name: Morty
characters.backstory:
Morty is the cleverest badger in the borough and the least interested in saying so. He keeps the watermill turning, he built the boiler the Science hall said would not hold, and he is always, without exception, in the middle of something — a sketch on the back of a flour docket, a gear cut too fine for anybody else's lathe, a governor he has taken apart twice this week because it was very nearly right.

The other half of him is dinner. Morty loves to eat, thinks about eating while he is working, and has never met a recipe he did not want to try once on principle. The mill kitchen is his: he grinds it, then he cooks it, and the animals who bring grain to the mill have learned to turn up hungry. He and Marmalade trade — a recipe against a mended oven door — and Morty takes notes on the recipe the way he takes notes on a bearing.

He is a Badger, so he builds things that survive the bad year. The boiler test is an annual embarrassment that the whole borough attends and nothing has ever gone wrong at it, which Morty regards as the point and everybody else regards as a shame.
characters.voice: Cheerful, technical, mouth half full. 'Hold on — hold on — right, try it now. Have you eaten?'
characters.arc: Morty braces the town and then feeds it. The Mill Kitchen Cook (1) is the cheap rung and the Badger signature: he has the town ready before the shock lands. The Watermill Mechanic (3) puts an animal back to work cheap, because he can always use a pair of paws. The Steam Engineer (4) braces the whole borough again from a boiler the Science hall said would not hold. The Master Millwright (5) is the mill running true: the first shift you complete each turn pays 1 more, every turn, for the rest of the game. Added since: a Grain Miller at 2 with no ability, and the arc's one rung in Agriculture — the plain half of the mill that has never gone wrong.

wantedArt.why: New job — Food at the end of a working mill. whiskerwood/9 is the Grain Miller on the mill floor, which is the machinery and not the stove; a badger in a flour-dusted apron cooking beside the gear housing would fix it.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_morty_mill_kitchen_cook_1 → the makerharvest atlas, tile 6. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Moss
characters.backstory:
Moss builds it his way. He has been told, by the guild, by the grange and once in writing by the Capital City, that the way is on the sheet; and Moss reads the sheet, puts it down, and does the thing that works. It has cost him two commissions and a formal warning and it has also given the borough a plough hitch that does not foul, a bridge arch a third lighter than the drawing, and a bench jig half the workshop now uses without knowing whose it was.

He is not a difficult animal about it, which is the confusing part. He is cheerful, he turns up, he takes the apprentice nobody else wants, and then he quietly builds it the other way and lets the result argue. About a third of the time the result loses and Moss rebuilds it properly and says so. The Town Workshop has stopped sending anybody to check.

Berry walked him through his first joint when he was twelve and has been the one animal Moss will listen to about anything ever since. What Berry actually taught him, Moss will tell you, was not the joint — it was that you work it out yourself, which is exactly what the guild now finds so annoying.
characters.voice: Easy, unbothered, already doing it. 'Yeah, that's the drawing. Watch this.'
characters.arc: Moss makes the town cheaper to build and harder to knock over, and he never once does it the way the sheet says. The Ploughwright (1) braces the borough. The Toolsmith (2) works a shift and the next Building comes in under the drawing. The Guild Architect (3) picks an animal back up out of Unemployment cheap. The Rocketwright (4) is Moss and Comet arguing productively. The Bridgewright (5) is the arch that should not stand: he is busy, and one of your Characters is on its feet because of what he worked out. Added since: a Timber Hand at 0 with no ability — Moss at eleven, before Berry got hold of him.

characters.name: Ned
characters.backstory:
Ned keeps the record, and the record is right. Every ward roll, every guild return, every date the bridge was out and every name on the hiring list since before Ned was born — filed, cross-referenced and correct, because a record that is nearly correct is a record that will one day be quoted by somebody who is nearly wrong.

They are by the book in the literal sense: the book exists, Ned wrote most of the current edition of it, and they will hand it to you open at the page rather than paraphrase. This makes them unpopular in a meeting and indispensable the following week. The borough's two standing arguments about the far hedgerow were both settled out of Ned's shelves in an afternoon, which is the kind of thing that stops being annoying the moment it is your argument.

What nobody sees is the putting by. A Squirrel archivist does not spend the find — Ned notices a discrepancy, files it, and says nothing for a year, and then the whole thing comes out at once, in order, with the dates. Lynnette prints what Ned certifies and has never had to print a correction.
characters.voice: Level, careful, allergic to 'roughly'. Says 'that is close, and it is not what happened'.
characters.arc: Ned files, and then Ned opens the file. The Page Runner (1) puts Supply by on every shift, the Squirrel's own slow start. The Night Archivist (2) sets the top of the deck in order. The Reference Librarian (4) does both — the order and another coin put by. The Chancellor of Records (5) is the year of quiet filing paid out in one go: every coin the town has put by, taken in at once, on the record. Added since: a Ward Recorder at 3 who draws off the turn's first Civics Event — the shelf opening on the ward's business.

characters.name: Oatmeal
characters.backstory:
Oatmeal is the oldest of nine, and it shows in everything he does. He was the one who counted heads at the door, who stood between the little ones and whatever was coming, who learned early that the way to keep everybody safe is to know the rules better than the trouble does. The habit never left him; it just got a desk.

He works for the town now — the ward office, the safety notices, the register of who lives where and who to call when the river comes up. Badgers dig in, and Oatmeal digs in on other animals' behalf: when a shock passes through the borough, the households that come through it unbothered are usually the ones he got to first. He is not fast and he is not clever about it. He is simply always already there.

Tuesdays he sings. The band is four of his own brothers and sisters and a Fox on the piano, the venue is whatever room will have them, and Oatmeal — who spends every other night of the week being the most responsible animal in the First Boroughs — stands up in front of a room and is, for an hour, somebody's favourite singer. His family has never missed a show.
characters.voice: Careful, unhurried, faintly official — until he is on a stage, where he is none of those things.
characters.arc: Civics is the duty: Ward Clerk (1) braces the town once, Safety Inspector (2) makes his neighbours untouchable for a turn, Town Warden (4) braces it every single turn, and Borough Alderman (5) does both at once for the whole town. Entertainment is the Tuesday: Jazz Singer (3) protects nobody from anything except despair, and turns out to be worth something anyway. Every ability is the same instinct — stand between the shock and whoever is behind you — and all of it is the Badger signature, `cancelReveal`, which is exactly what the charter says a Badger is for.

wantedVerbs.why: 'Protecting other animals' wants a shield another Mayor's Characters could also stand behind; every protective verb in the engine is scoped to the player who plays the card.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Protected his own town instead — `cancelReveal` for shared shocks and `unemploymentShield` for effects, which is the same instinct within the rules.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built, on the maker's instruction and with the help to the rival kept rather than designed out. `protectCharacter: { everyone: true }` shelters one Character in *each* town, both Mayors choosing for themselves, and the shelter is now a great deal more than untargetability: nothing takes a sheltered animal out of their town while the cover holds — not a rival's removal and not weather that falls on both towns — and `turns` says how many of that Mayor's turns it holds for. That it helps the rival is the price of it being that good, and the power model prices it that way: a shared shelter pays its owner 0.4 of a private one. Oatmeal's Awning is the Event and The Long Awning is the Town Building that puts it up again every time anybody is put out of work.

wantedArt.why: No painted tile shows anyone on a stage. With no `art` set, a Badger character falls back to the painted Badger workbench scene rather than the new Entertainment backdrop — the painted species tile always wins over the drawn one. An open-mic painting would fix it.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_oatmeal_jazz_singer_3 → the makercivic atlas, tile 1, and a Full Art portrait of its own. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Orien
characters.backstory:
Orien counts things. He has counted things since he was small enough to be lifted onto the Counting House steps to wait for somebody, and he has never found a reason to stop. What the borough took a while to understand is that he is not doing it for anyone. He does it the way other animals whittle. He came home from his first week of paid work with a table of every price the Capital City had taken that season, drawn out in four colours, for nobody.

There is a machine in the back room of his house. He built it out of what the Observatory threw away and what Patch would sell him, and it has been rebuilt four times since; it clicks all evening and most of the night, and it is the reason he is never at the bonfire. Into it go the shift returns, the auction prices, the ferry's crossings, the weight of every cart Liz has ever put on her plate. Out of it come the tables the almanac prints — Lynnette sets them, Orien supplies them, and nobody in the borough has ever paid for a figure since. Ask him what a Building will go for and he will tell you, and he will be within a Supply, and he will be a little put out if you sound surprised.

He is not good with animals, which he knows, and which he has decided is a fair trade. He has been made a committee's figures badger eleven times and has never once been asked to speak. He likes it best when a meeting goes quiet and looks at him, and he can put a number on the table and go home.
characters.voice: Precise, cheerful, and a little too fast. Answers the question you should have asked. Says 'well — it depends what you mean by cheap' and then tells you, at length, what it depends on.
characters.arc: Five jobs, one habit: Orien changes what a thing costs. The Tally Clerk at 0 works out a cheaper way to hire the next animal and hands the note over. The Rate Checker at 2 has read the lot before you challenged it, so challenging is cheaper. The Borough Actuary at 3 prices the Capital City's Buildings a season ahead, and the town buys under the number. The Survey Computer at 4 is the machine at full tilt: every shift the town finishes that turn pays more than it should. The Town Planner at 5 is what all of it was for: he sits down with the whole borough's figures and the next animal through the door comes in well under budget.

wantedArt.why: The Survey Computer is a new job: a badger at a home-built calculating engine at two in the morning, tape everywhere. townlife/2 is the bridge engineer's site and is the wrong room entirely.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_orien_survey_computer_4 → the townlife atlas, tile 2. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

wantedVerbs.why: The story wants Orien's tables to pay the town a standing rate — every shift, every turn, because the figures are simply better now.
wantedVerbs.workaround: A turn-long `shiftBonus` mod on the cost-4, re-applied each turn he is upright. Same outcome while he is working, and it stops when he does.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as the `townShiftBonus` passive, which carries a value: every shift the town finishes pays that much more while the rule is in force. The Survey Computer no longer re-applies a turn-long mod each morning — the figures are simply better now, and they stop being better the moment he sits down. `passiveTotal` in state.js is the general form of `hasPassive` for a standing rule with a quantity.

characters.name: Osh
characters.backstory:
Osh goes round the borough with a treadle wheel on a handcart and puts an edge back on things. Knives, shears, billhooks, the mill's dressing picks, the bakery's scrapers, one ceremonial sword that has never cut anything. He does a circuit that takes eleven days and has done it in the same order since he was small enough to need a box to stand on.

He is a mouse and the wheel is nearly as big as he is, which the borough finds funnier than he does. Morty's mill kitchen and Marmalade's bakery are both on day four.
characters.voice: Quiet, exact, and briefly unbearable about other animals' edges.
characters.arc: Two rungs, both of them the wheel. At 0 he is on somebody else's round; at 2 it is his round, his order and his eleven days, which is why the second card works the long shift for more.

wantedArt.why: Osh is a new animal and no painted tile shows this job. With no `art` set the cards fall back to the painted Mouse scene, which is the right species doing the wrong work.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_osh_sharpener_s_boy_0 → the makerworkshop atlas, tile 7; mk_osh_edge_grinder_2 → the makerworkshop atlas, tile 8. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Otter Pup
characters.backstory:
There is an Otter Pup under the counter at the All-Night Café most nights and Bean has never once asked whose. They come in off the ferry steps with the lightermen, they are handed something warm, and they are put to work carrying it two tables over, which takes an extremely long time and involves the entire room.

Three days for one Supply is a terrible rate for an Otter, a species that does nothing slowly. That is rather the point: an Otter Pup is the only slow thing an Otter is ever going to be, and the borough lets them have it.
characters.voice: Breathless, sideways, already halfway to the next thing.
characters.arc: The one slow rung on the fastest ladder in the borough, and a post any Otter may be found standing in afterwards.

wantedArt.want: Otter Pup: Dylan carried one across the counter on a tray and both of them behaved as though that were the ordinary way to cross a room.

characters.name: Owlet
characters.backstory:
Owlets are awake, which in the First Boroughs is a qualification. They are taken on the night round at an age the day borough would find alarming, carried where the lamps are lit, and told what each thing is once. Owls are told things once.

Three days for a single Supply is the worst rate on the board and no Owl has ever apologised for it. An Owlet is not being paid for the work. An Owlet is being paid for the fourteen years of knowing which window has a light in it at three in the morning, and the borough settles up a long way down the line.
characters.voice: Enormous, unblinking, and a question you were not ready for.
characters.arc: An Owlet counts for two when an Owl is set over them: the night round is half of what any Owl in this borough knows.

wantedArt.want: Owlet: Mandee carries the lanterns and lets an Owlet hold the pole. The Owlet has never once dropped it, and has been told so exactly once.

characters.name: Patch
characters.backstory:
Patch went into the Salvage Yard as a kit because there was money in it if you were small enough to get under things and quick enough to get out again. That was the whole of the plan for about two years. Then he sold a mangle back to the animal who had thrown it away, for more than it had cost new, because he had put a new roller in it — and he understood, standing there with the coin in his paw, that the diving was the least interesting part of the business.

So he built the rest of it. He takes it out, he sorts it, he mends what is worth mending and improves what is worth improving, and he sells it back to the borough at a price nobody has ever complained about. Annabelle takes the paper — that is hers, and the two of them have never once discussed it — and Patch takes everything else. What he is really known for now is the judging. Animals bring him things and ask whether they are worth keeping, and he turns them over twice and tells them, and he is right. Word got round, and now they bring him other things to ask the same question about: a trade, a lease, a season that has not gone well, somebody they are not sure about. He turns those over twice as well.

He will tell you he is not qualified, which is true, and that he is only a raccoon with a yard, which is also true, and then he will tell you to keep the lease and sell the cart, and you will, and it will have been the right way round.
characters.voice: Unhurried, dry, entirely certain. Asks two questions and then gives you the answer. Says 'that's worth keeping' and 'that isn't, and you know it isn't' in exactly the same tone.
characters.arc: The business, built upward out of the bins. The Junkyard Diver at 0 is the kit under the pile, and every shift he works the town puts something up cheaper out of what he dragged home. The Salvage Sorter at 2 has a bench and a price list, so what the town raises next comes in cheaper. The Valuer at 3 is the job the borough actually made for him: he goes through the Dump and comes back with the thing and the reason. The Yard Foreman at 4 runs the whole yard, so every shift he finishes turns something discarded into something standing. The Reclamation Merchant at 5 is the far end of the mangle: he takes out of the Dump and puts up cheap, and the town's next Building is half somebody else's old one.

wantedArt.why: The Valuer is the yard's counter, not the town hall: an animal handing a broken thing over a plank and waiting for the verdict. neighbors/4 is the salvage portrait and is close, but the scene is the counter.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_patch_valuer_3 → the neighbors atlas, tile 4. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for abilities about swapping Buildings: return a Building your town has raised to the City Dump and raise another in its place, which is exactly Patch's trade — the old mangle out, the mended one in.
wantedVerbs.workaround: The two halves of the swap, built from verbs that exist: `takeFromCityDump` takes the Market card back out of the shared Dump, and a `buildingDiscount` mod makes putting the replacement up cheap. The town ends up with the better Building; it just cannot hand the old one back.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `swapBuilding`: one of your Buildings comes down — a bought one to the City Dump, a built one home to your own Town Dump — and a Building somebody else threw away goes up in the place it left. Both halves or neither, so a town with nothing up has nothing to trade and an empty Dump nothing to trade for. The old mangle out, the mended one in, and the Reclamation Merchant is the card that does it.

characters.name: Peanut
characters.backstory:
Peanut keeps the books, and has kept them since they were small enough to need two paws for the ledger. Half the borough's accounts pass through them: the grange's feed bills, the ferry's tolls, the guild's quarterly returns. Peanut is bright in the plain way that gets noticed late — they find the error, they find the cheaper supplier, and they tell you about both, cheerfully, whether or not you asked.

The café came second and turned out to be the point. Peanut took the day counter at Bean's family coffeehouse by the Hiring Hall — mostly to have somewhere to spread the ledgers out, and because Bean needed somebody steady behind it — and discovered that if you give the whole town coffee they will tell you what everything costs. Now the café is the office. The accounts get done between orders, the good deals get passed across the counter with the change, and a working animal who stops in for a cup leaves knowing something they did not know before.

What Peanut is bad at is spending. Everything goes by — in the till, in the tin, in the café cash box — against a rainy day that a Squirrel is always sure is coming. The town is richer for Peanut and Peanut is poor most of the year, right up until the moment they are not.

Peanut does not own the café and has never wanted to. It is Bean's, inherited and held on to with both wings; Peanut keeps its books, works its counter and, on the days Bean is coming apart, quietly runs it.
characters.voice: Warm, quick, faintly bookkeeperish. Gives you the number and then the kinder version of the number. Never says 'no', says 'not this quarter'.
characters.arc: Commerce is the career: Ledger Apprentice (0) learns to put a little by, Accountant (2) learns to call it back in when it is needed, Town Comptroller (5) stops working their own desk and makes every animal in town a little better paid. Food is the room the career happens in: Barista (1) takes a coin off every shift that passes the counter, Café Manager (4) turns the café into the place friends are hired from. The 0 and the 1 are deliberately small — the Squirrel hole is slow starts, and Peanut's whole story is that the payoff is later.

wantedVerbs.why: The Comptroller wants every Character's shift to pay +1 as a standing rule; `shiftBonus` is a player-level mod that `consumeMod` spends on the next shift only, so it cannot express a permanent per-shift bonus.
