wantedVerbs.workaround: Used an `onShiftCompleted` ability with no `self` condition, which fires for every shift the player completes and gains 1 Supply — the same outcome, logged per shift rather than folded into the shift's output.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Not built, deliberately: the Comptroller's `onShiftCompleted` ability already produces exactly the asked-for outcome (+1 on every shift you complete), and a second mechanism for the same thing would be two ways to say one sentence.

wantedVerbs.why: The Café Manager wanted 'your Food and Commerce Characters cost 1 less to recruit'; `recruitDiscount` is untyped and applies to the next recruit of any kind.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Left the discount untyped and put the character in the flavor instead.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: a mod may carry a `filter`, and `recruitCost` only counts the mods that match the animal being recruited. The Café Manager's discount is good for Food and Commerce.

wantedArt.why: No painted tile shows a Squirrel behind a counter. nightworkers tile 2 is Bean's café, but Bean is an Owl. With no `art` set they fall back to the painted Squirrel forager scene, not the new Food backdrop — the painted species tile always wins over the drawn one. A Squirrel behind a counter would fix it.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_peanut_barista_1 → the makercivic atlas, tile 0, and a Full Art portrait of its own; mk_peanut_cafe_manager_4 → the makerborough atlas, tile 2. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Pebble
characters.backstory:
The crossing has been Pebble's family's for seven generations. Their father had it, and his father, and his grandmother before that, and her daughter after her, and the borough long ago stopped bothering with the names: whoever is on the boat is the ferryotter, and the ferryotter is whoever is on the boat. Most families with a thing like that behind them produce, sooner or later, somebody who wants out. Pebble's family has been waiting three generations for that animal and it is not going to be Pebble.

They like it. That is the whole of it, and it takes some animals a while to believe. Four crossings an hour, the same bank, the same rope, the same eleven regulars and their eleven opinions, and Pebble goes home at the end of it perfectly content. Brooke, who is climbing the ladder out of exactly this job toward the River Otter licence, has asked them about it directly, twice. Pebble said that standing where their father stood, doing what their father did, with his grandmother's fare chits still in the tin, is not a thing you climb out of. The chits are the other half of it: their family struck their own, a worn wooden otter on a round of hard wood, handed to every passenger and counted back at the far bank. Half the borough has one in a pocket that they never handed back, and the rest of the town's chits — the study marks, the building marks — are copies of the ferry's.

They are not ambitious and they are not bored, and both of those facts make the Harbourmaster's office slightly uneasy. Willow has offered Pebble the warden's post three times. Pebble took it on the third offer on the condition that it did not mean giving up the boat.
characters.voice: Easy, unhurried, entirely without edge. Talks about their great-grandmother in the present tense by accident. Says 'mind the step' about four hundred times a day and means it every time.
characters.arc: One job, four generations deep, and every rung hands out more of the family's chits. The Crossing Hand at 0 earns one a shift. The Bridge Courier at 1 hands one over with the fare and has somebody else up and moving by morning. The Ferry Master at 3 is the boat at full tempo — the shift slides from paw to paw, Otter-fashion, and a chit goes into the tin with it. The Harbour Warden at 5 is Willow's post, taken on the third asking and only on terms: a chit every turn, and once the tin is deep enough the crossing pays the town as well as the family.

wantedVerbs.why: The story wants a chit for every animal who crosses — a token per Character the town readies or moves, not a flat one per shift.
wantedVerbs.workaround: A fixed `gainToken` count on each version, rising with the rung. The tin fills at the same rate on a busy turn and a quiet one, which is the one thing a ferry never does.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `gainToken: { per: "charactersReadied" }`: a chit for every animal who actually crossed. `p.turn.readied` counts the Characters who have stood up in this town this turn — in the Ready phase or by any effect that put one back on its feet — and the Harbour Warden reads it at the end of the turn, when the count is what really happened. A busy turn fills the tin and a quiet one does not, which is the one thing a ferry never used to do.

characters.name: Peter
characters.backstory:
Peter lays hedges. He was born at the far end of the borough within sight of the far hedgerow and has spent his working life inside it: cutting the stems most of the way through, bending them over while they are still living, pegging them down and letting them grow back into a wall. It takes a winter to do a field's length and about fifteen years to find out whether you did it properly.

This is why the borough's hedges are harder to take down than they look. Maribel files the objection at the meeting; Peter is the reason there is still something there to object about. The two of them have never discussed it.
characters.voice: Slow, practical, mostly about the hedge. Answers a question about himself with an answer about the hedge.
characters.arc: Two rungs and no tricks at all, which is the maker's brief for him: the lad with the billhook at 0, and the hedgelayer whose winter's work will still be standing in fifteen years at 3. The long shift is the whole of the second card — a hedge is not laid in a turn, and Peter is paid for what is there at the end of it.

wantedArt.why: Peter is a new animal and no painted tile shows this job. With no `art` set the cards fall back to the painted Rabbit scene, which is the right species doing the wrong work.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_peter_hedge_cutter_0 → the makerharvest atlas, tile 8; mk_peter_hedgelayer_3 → the makerharvest atlas, tile 9. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Pockets
characters.backstory:
Pockets taught Patch to dive. That is the fact he leads with, and it is true, and it has been getting steadily less useful to him for about fifteen years. He was first into the Salvage Yard, first under the pile, first to work out which of the Capital City's carters would take a bent thing off you at the gate and ask nothing; and then his little brother put a new roller in a mangle, and built a business, and got a counter and a price list and a reputation for telling animals the truth about their leases, and Pockets did not.

What he got instead was range. There is nothing in the borough's dumps he cannot get back out and very little he cannot find a buyer for, including things the buyer should not have and things that were never anybody's to sell. He works the City Dump the way his brother works the yard, except that Patch sells you back your own mangle, mended, and Pockets sells you somebody else's, and does not say whose. Nothing he does is quite a crime. Several things he does are the shape of one, seen from a distance, in poor light.

The brothers are on speaking terms. Pockets turns up at the yard about four times a year, is fed, and leaves with something; Patch has never once asked what for, which is the nearest thing to forgiveness either of them goes in for. The borough hires Pockets when it wants a thing back that it has already thrown away, and is careful not to ask how, and pays him in the same careful way.
characters.voice: Quick, charming, all shoulders. Answers the question next to the one you asked. Says 'now I never said that' about things he has just said.
characters.arc: Three rungs, all of them the same trade at increasing nerve. The Kerbside Dealer at 1 gets an Event back out of your own Town Dump — small, legitimate, his brother's method. The Odd-Lot Dealer at 3 works the shared City Dump as well and comes back with both. The Salvage Raccoon at 4 is hired out of the Capital City by a town that wants something back and has decided not to ask how.

wantedArt.why: The Odd-Lot Dealer is a raccoon at the gate at dusk with a barrow under a sheet, dealing with a carter who is not getting down. neighbors/4 is the salvage portrait his brother already uses.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_pockets_odd_lot_dealer_3 → the neighbors atlas, tile 4. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for an Event or a Building out of the City Dump. The Building half exists — `takeFromCityDump` — but an Event in the City Dump cannot be reached at all: Events go to a town's own Dump, and nothing on either shelf crosses from one town's Dump to the other's.
wantedVerbs.workaround: The two Dumps he can reach: `eventFromDumpToHand` for the Event, out of your own Town Dump, and `takeFromCityDump` for the Market card. It is the same pair of hands doing the same trick; it just never goes through the rival's bin.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `eventFromOpponentDump`, which is the half that was genuinely unreachable: an Event in the rival's own Town Dump, into your hand. Events still never reach the City Dump — that would be a different card type in a different bin — so the Odd-Lot Dealer now works the two bins that actually have something in them: the shared City Dump for a Market card, and the rival's for the Event they have already shown you is worth playing.

characters.name: Quill
characters.backstory:
Quill's parents had the orchard and their parents had it before that, and Quill grew up in it — under it, mostly, in the long grass between the rows, being handed up windfalls. When it came to her she did not have to decide anything, which she is aware is a kind of luck other animals do not get. She could not imagine doing anything else and has never tried very hard to.

What she has decided, over and over, is that the orchard should be full. An orchard does not need thirty animals in it; hers has thirty animals in it anyway, most weekends, because she cannot bear the rows to be quiet. There is a cider social in the barn from September to about February and a bonfire whenever the prunings get above knee height, which is more often than pruning strictly requires. She invents reasons. Half the borough has picked for her one autumn, and about a third of them turned up for a Saturday and were still there at the end of the week, on the books, being paid.

That is the other thing the orchard does, and Quill will not be thanked for it. Rosabeth's garden takes the animals who have stopped getting up and mends them; the orchard takes everybody, all the time, whether or not anything is wrong, which means a hedgehog who is quietly out of work can be in the rows on Saturday morning without ever having admitted to anything. The Hiring Hall knows. It sends them. Quill pretends not to have noticed, hands them a basket, and puts the kettle on for thirty.
characters.voice: Loud, delighted, always catering for more animals than are present. Ends most sentences with 'come Saturday'. Never asks whether you are all right; asks whether you can carry a ladder.
characters.arc: The orchard, filling up. The Orchard Hand at 0 gets one animal into the rows where nothing can reach them. The Orchard Keeper at 2 is the standing rule of the place: nobody who is here loses their place here. The Cider Maker at 3 is the barn in September — the social pays, and somebody under the rafters is safe for the evening. The Orchard Scribe at 4 keeps the book of which tree fruited when, which is also the book of who picked, and the whole orchard holds while she is busy. The Harvest Steward at 5 is the season entire: the rows full, the books shut, and not one animal in them out of work.

wantedArt.why: The Cider Maker is the barn in September with the press going and thirty animals in it — a Food scene the orchard tiles (neighbors/9, the keeper among the trees) do not have.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_quill_cider_maker_3 → the nightskies atlas, tile 9. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Quinn
characters.backstory:
Quinn is at everything. The ward meeting, the boundary hearing, the reading of a will, the argument at the weighbridge, the bad meeting after the bridge went — Quinn was at the back of all of them with the book open, and Quinn said nothing at any of them. He has been the borough's scrivener for as long as anyone can produce a date for, which is itself a small joke, because if anybody could produce a date it would be him.

He is not unfriendly. He answers if you ask him something, in about four words, and then goes back to it. The trouble is that a great many animals have said something in a room he was in and watched his pen move, and it is an unsettling thing to be recorded by somebody who will not tell you what he made of it. Two or three of the older animals will not sit with their backs to him. The children, on the other hand, adore him: there is a settled belief among the borough's young that Quinn is a mage, on the grounds that the writing comes out faster than the talking goes in, and that he was seen at the fair, the regatta and the Hiring Hall on the same afternoon. Inkwell, who has a rumour of his own and has never denied it either, was asked once to settle it. Inkwell said only that Quinn writes faster than he does.

What the book is actually for is this. When a place falls vacant the Hiring Hall comes to Quinn, and Quinn turns back four years and finds the animal who did that exact work in a bad winter and has not been asked since, and writes the name on a slip, and hands it over, and says nothing. More animals in this borough have been got back into work by that slip than by any committee sitting.
characters.voice: Four words at most, and all four load-bearing. Writes while you are still talking. When he does speak it lands in a quiet room and is usually a date.
characters.arc: Three rungs, one book, pointed at Unemployment. The Meeting Scribe at 1 is at the back of the room, and a finished shift gets one animal back in cheap. The Town Scrivener at 3 is the post as the Capital City hires it, and the Mouse signature with it: whatever was written down comes back out of the Dump. The Keeper of the Record at 5 is the whole archive open: he turns back four years and the right name comes back for nothing.

wantedArt.why: The Keeper of the Record is the archive at night, one mouse and four years of shelving open at once. capital/4 is the Capital City's hiring portrait and is the job below it.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_quinn_keeper_of_the_record_5 → the capital atlas, tile 4. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Raccoon Kit
characters.backstory:
The Salvage Yard has a shelf at knee height that nobody stocks and that is never empty. That is the Kits' shelf. What is on it has been carried in from the City Dump one piece at a time by animals too small to carry two, and Pockets prices it exactly as seriously as anything else in the yard.

Three days of a Raccoon Kit is one Supply, which is a poor rate and about right for somebody who stops to look at everything on the way. The looking is the job. A Raccoon who has not spent a season finding out what the borough throws away will never be much of a Raccoon, and Pockets got the ward to count the shelf at two on exactly that argument.
characters.voice: Delighted, in detail, about something that was in a bin.
characters.arc: A Raccoon Kit counts for two when a Raccoon is set over them: a season on the City Dump road is half of what any Raccoon in this borough knows.

wantedArt.want: Raccoon Kit: Pockets gave one a ha'penny for a doorknob with no door. It is still on the shelf. It is still, Pockets maintains, worth a ha'penny.

characters.name: Reese
characters.backstory:
Reese flies, and Reese is aware that Reese flies. The sunglasses are worn indoors. The yellow pleather coat is worn in August. He walks into the Hiring Hall the way other animals walk into a room they have just bought, and the infuriating thing — the thing that has kept the borough from ever quite getting a word in — is that he is exactly as good as he says he is.

He came up the way Raccoons come up, which is out of the yard: the first aircraft he ever touched was three aircraft, and none of the three had all of its parts. He can still tell you what came off which. He holds the borough's only instrument ticket, he is the one who goes when the weather has shut the ferry, and he has never in his life said that a flight was difficult.

What he will admit to, once, late, is that he checks the City Dump before every trip. Not for spares. For the lists — the manifests and the freight notes the Capital City throws out — because a Raccoon reads the bins and the bins are where the borough says what it is actually doing. He would rather you thought it was instinct.
characters.voice: Unbothered, three-quarters of a beat slow, and never takes the glasses off.
characters.arc: The cheap Reese is still scavenging; the dear ones are the animal who fetches out of the shared bin and then goes and flies, which is the whole species in one coat.

wantedArt.want: Every version of Reese.

characters.name: Roger
characters.backstory:
Roger can fix things. Not one kind of thing — the lock, the lease, the rota, the argument between the two carters, the reason the ward's accounts do not add up — and he does it without much fuss and usually on the way to somewhere else. The borough has noticed. The borough's response to noticing an animal like that is always the same, and Roger has been made chair, warden, clerk, judge and ombudsman of one thing or another since he was about twenty-two, every single time by a room turning round and looking at him.

He is bad at it. Not at the work — at the office. The job of a chair is to decide, and deciding means one of the two animals in front of you walks out having lost, and Roger cannot do it. He sees it from where they are standing. He sees it from where the other one is standing too, immediately and completely, and he sits there with both of them true at once and the room waiting. He has adjourned hearings to think about it for a week. He has found for both sides in writing, twice, which Ned had to file as two documents.

What the borough worked out, eventually, is the ha'penny. When a call is genuinely even Roger takes it out, and somebody else calls it in the air, and whatever it does is what happens, and Roger writes it down and everyone goes home. He has never once called it himself. He says that would be taking a side. The ha'penny is worn almost smooth now and it has settled four boundary questions, a dispute about a bandstand, and who was to have the good pitch at the fair, and the borough considers all four of those settled forever.
characters.voice: Mild, apologetic, extremely capable. Starts sentences with 'well, the thing is, from where he's sitting —'. Says 'that's fair' to both animals in the same conversation and means it both times.
characters.arc: Five rungs and one worn ha'penny. The Locksmith at 1 is the fixing, before anyone made an office of it — and even then a tie pays him. The Records Clerk at 2 is the borough's paperwork and the Fox's eye on the Capital City. The Circuit Judge at 3 is the first real bench, where a tie starts paying properly. The Fair Broker at 4 is the animal in the middle of a bidding war who can push his own side once the room has stalled. The Ombudsman at 5 is the whole of it: he wins the ties he cannot decide, and every one of them pays.

wantedArt.why: The Fair Broker is two traders and a fox between them with a coin in the air. neighbors/6 is the bench portrait and boroughs/2 is the lock bench; neither has the toss in it.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_roger_fair_broker_4 → the neighbors atlas, tile 6. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for chance: an effect that tosses Roger's ha'penny and does one thing on heads and another on tails — the borough's actual method for a call that will not come down on its own.
wantedVerbs.workaround: The one genuine coin toss the engine already has: the tied bid. `onTiedBid` fires exactly when two Mayors have put up the same number and neither is right, which is the situation Roger is for, and everything he does hangs off it. It is chance the players walked into rather than chance he can call on demand.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `coinFlip`: `{ heads, tails }`, each side an effect of its own. It draws on the same seeded rng every shuffle uses, so a game is still replayable from its seed and the toss goes in the log rather than hiding inside the effect. The Fair Broker tosses on a tied bid, which is still the situation he is for — but the ha'penny is a real one now, and somebody else calls it, exactly as his flavor always said.

characters.name: Rosabeth
characters.backstory:
Rosabeth talks to her plants. She sings to them too, and on a good morning she dances down the rows doing it, and she has been doing this for thirty years in full view of a borough that gave up being surprised about it some time in the second decade. There is a persistent and not entirely unfair joke that she likes the garden better than the animals in it. Rosabeth has heard the joke and finds it funny and has never bothered to correct it.

She ought to be correcting it, because the whole point of the garden is the shelf it fills. Rosabeth's tinctures are half herb and half something she will describe as the moon, or the mood of the bed, or what the rosemary told her, and they are the only remedies in the First Boroughs that reliably work. Nobody can account for it. The Science hall has been through her notes twice and come away with a list of ingredients and no method. She is entirely relaxed about this and says the method is the singing.

What she is actually for, and what the borough forgets to say out loud, is getting animals back on their feet. An animal who has lost a place and stopped getting up in the morning ends up at Rosabeth's gate sooner or later, usually sent by somebody, and Rosabeth puts a mug of something in their paws and sets them to work on the beds until they are fit to be somewhere else. Half the Hiring Hall's second chances started in that garden. She charges for the tincture and never for the rest of it.
characters.voice: Warm, dreamy, faintly sing-song. Talks to the plants mid-conversation and does not treat it as an interruption. Absolutely certain about things she cannot explain.
characters.arc: Four versions and one job under all of them: getting an animal back into work. It escalates by how much of the cost she absorbs — at 0 a shift in the garden knocks a Supply off the next rehire, at 2 she brings somebody back herself for a Supply less, at 5 she brings them back for nothing and reads something out of it besides. The Apothecary at 3 is the one card that does not rehire, and it keeps the Mouse's signature: every recipe comes back out of the Town Dump eventually, because Rosabeth never throws a recipe away. Added since: a Garden Hand at 1 with no ability — the animal who was sent to her gate, working the beds and not yet able to do anything for anybody.

wantedVerbs.verb: `rehire` with a filter on who it can bring back
wantedVerbs.why: `rehire` filters only on cost (`cost`, `maxCost`). Rosabeth's garden takes the animal who has been down longest, not the cheapest one, and the story wanted to say so — oldest in Unemployment, or a Character of a named study.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Left the choice open on every rehire: the Mayor picks, which reads as Rosabeth taking whoever came to the gate.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `rehire` reads `filter.study`, `filter.species` and `filter.minCost` alongside the cost filters it always had. The Herbalist Physician now brings back an Agriculture animal specifically — the ones the garden is actually for — rather than whoever happens to be cheapest.

characters.name: Sage
characters.backstory:
Sage learned to read on the Lending Library's low shelf, which is where the scientific romances live — the penny serials about the other side of the sky, rockets the shape of a thumb, animals on a red world who are polite and terrifying. They read the lot before they were ten and then read them again, and they have never entirely stopped. Everything Sage knows about the sky started as somebody's invention, and the fact that some of it turned out to be true is, they will tell you, the best thing that has ever happened to anybody.

So they took the dome. Sage keeps the borough's watch list — what is due, what is late, what has not been seen since a year nobody here was alive for — and they keep it to the minute. The Crown wanted to know when the comet would come and Sage told them to the minute and then went back to bed. Sota grinds the lenses and has no interest whatever in what they are pointed at; Sage is the opposite animal, and the two of them work the same bench for whole nights without either saying anything the other wants to hear.

And they will not go. The selection board has left the application form on Sage's desk three times, flat, unmentioned, the way you leave a thing for somebody who has said no politely. Sage knows the space division better than the space division does — they have read the manifests, they sit in on the launch meetings, they are the animal Comet writes to from the pad — and they have never once put a name on the form. It is very high up, they say, and there is no one to tell if something goes wrong, and anyway somebody has to be down here looking, or what is the point of anyone going.
characters.voice: Precise about numbers, hopeless about wonder — a forecast to the minute and then a sentence about what it would be like to stand there. Says "somebody has to be looking" the way other animals say sorry.
characters.arc: Three rungs and one dome. The Night Assistant at 0 reads ahead in the town's own deck. The Astronomer at 3 reads the Capital City too, because the sky and the market both come round on a schedule. The Royal Astronomer at 5 does all of it every morning and draws what comes of it: the watch list that the Crown pays for.

wantedVerbs.why: Sage's whole gift is knowing the order things arrive in; the story wanted them to put the Capital City's deck back in a chosen order the way `reorderDeckTop` does for a town's own deck. `peekMarketDeck` only looks.
wantedVerbs.workaround: They look at the Market Deck and reorder their own — the borough's side of the sky, which is the half Sage is allowed to touch.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `peekMarketDeck` takes `reorder`, and the look at the Capital City's deck ends with the watcher putting it back the way they want it. Sage's top rung carries it — the Royal Astronomer sets the order the Capital City deals in at the start of every turn — and so does the Star Party, where the whole borough is out on the hill looking at the same sky. The Astronomer at 3 still only looks, which is what makes the promotion mean something.

characters.name: Scott
characters.backstory:
Scott writes it all down and then sells it back to the borough in pamphlets. Half of what comes off Lynnette's press with his name on it is invention — dragons under the far hedgerow, a lighterman who bargains with the river, the winter the moon came down for a look — and the other half is the plain truth about what the borough did in 1841, with the dates right. He does not keep the two apart on the shelf, and he will not be drawn on which sells better.

The rule he does keep is that the true half is true. Everything he writes about a real animal or a real year goes across Ned's shelves first, and Ned certifies it or Scott cuts it, and in fifteen years Lynnette has never had to print a correction to anything of his. It makes him slow. It also means that when Scott says the bridge went in a particular spring, the borough stops arguing about which spring. What it never makes him is dull: he has worked out, over a long career, exactly where in a ward-boundary dispute to put a joke about somebody's uncle, and exactly where in a reading for the little ones to put a fart.

He collects more than he prints. Every market between here and the Capital City, every lighterman coming off a night run, every old animal on a bench — he takes the story, pays for it with a better one, and puts it by. Most of it goes into the tin and stays there for years. When a season finally calls for it, he opens the tin, and it turns out he has had the answer since about a decade ago.
characters.voice: Warm, digressive, always three sentences from a joke. Starts things with 'now, this is the true one' and means it about half the time, on purpose.
characters.arc: Collect, print, verify, pay out — a Squirrel's shape, which is to say poor for a long time and then suddenly not. The Story Collector at 0 works the markets and puts everything by. The Pamphleteer at 2 is the press run: he sets the top of the deck the way he sets a page, and knows what is coming next. The Town Chronicler at 3 is the Ned years, slow and unarguable: he orders his own deck and watches the Capital City's at the same time. The Natural Historian at 4 goes out after the things nobody has written down yet and puts more by. The Author of the Boroughs at 5 opens the tin: a lifetime of collecting, cashed in at once, which is exactly what a Squirrel is for.

wantedArt.why: The Pamphleteer is the press floor at Lynnette's with a squirrel reading a wet proof, not the road: neighbors/15 is the travelling storyteller and is the previous job.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_scott_pamphleteer_2 → the neighbors atlas, tile 15. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Shay
characters.backstory:
Shay is the borough's doctor, and she is the reason the Science hall and Rosabeth's garden are on speaking terms. She reads everything — the county papers, the Capital City's returns, the three medical journals that come up on the late ferry and are addressed to nobody in particular — and she reads them the night they arrive, because she is an Owl and the night is when the reading gets done. Whatever is new, Shay has already read about it, and has usually already written to somebody about it.

She keeps a surgery two doors from the Physic Garden and does her rounds twice: once through the borough, and once across the ward boundary, because an animal asleep on their feet is an animal asleep on their feet whichever Mayor's town they happen to be standing in. This has been raised at meetings. It has never once been stopped.

The other half of her week is paint. She works small, quickly, and in a great deal of green, and she takes what she has done to the farmer's market on a trestle with a price card on it. It is the only part of her life she will admit to doing badly, and she does it every week, which the borough has quietly noticed is what she tells everybody else to do.

characters.name: Sota
characters.backstory:
Sota grinds glass. Every lens in the Observatory's smaller instruments came off their bench, and the two big ones have been re-seated by them twice. It is months of work to take a blank down to a figure that will hold a star still, and the last of it is done by hand, by feel, at about the speed of a plant growing.

They have been invited to look through the finished article on many occasions and have gone each time out of politeness. What Sota wants to know is whether the edge is right. What the star is doing is the Observatory's business.

The touchline was Teresa's idea and Sota has never given the borough a reason for saying yes beyond the light being better out there than over a blank. They assist. They do not shout — they have never shouted at anything — and they move two paces up the line and the whole back four moves with them, and in six seasons nobody has managed to see the signal.
characters.voice: Soft, unhurried, entirely uninterested in the sky.
characters.arc: Glass at one end and the touchline at the other, and the same animal doing both at the same speed: the cheap versions stand next to Teresa, the dear ones are the bench the Observatory cannot replace.

characters.name: Squirrel Kit
characters.backstory:
A Squirrel Kit is given a tin. That is the entire ceremony. What goes in the tin is the Kit's business and nobody else's, and a Squirrel who has not learned by the end of the first winter that a tin put by in October is worth four times a tin spent in October has not learned the only thing Squirrels teach.

They produce almost nothing for three days at a stretch, and the borough has never minded, because a Squirrel town is poor all game and rich exactly once. A Kit is the first half of that sentence, standing in a doorway holding a tin — and the ward records the post at the bottom of the ladder, because a Squirrel who has only had one winter has not yet done the part that counts.
characters.voice: Counting under their breath, and not telling you the number.
characters.arc: The tin is the whole of the trade and the trade takes a lifetime, so the ward credits the first winter with nothing at all. Any Squirrel may be played over a Kit.

characters.name: Squirt
characters.backstory:
Squirt has the lower room, the shorter fuse and the better legs, and he is out of the door at the bell because the borough side trains at five. He is a genuinely good player — left wing, twenty years of it — and he is the reason the school's afternoon is organised the way it is, which the school has never formally admitted.

The swapping is mostly his idea. Dirt goes along with it; Squirt starts it, usually about ten minutes into something he has decided is boring. The two of them have run this borough's oldest joke for so long that it has stopped being a joke and become a sort of civic weather.

On the pitch he stops being funny entirely, which is the thing about him that surprises animals who only know him from the ward meetings. Teresa shouts at him from the touchline and he does exactly what she says. Sota, who says nothing at all, he also does exactly what they say. He has been asked how he can tell the two of them apart and has said, without smiling, that it is easy: one of them is loud.
characters.voice: Fast, cheerful, and gone before the end of your sentence.
characters.arc: The school rungs are the swap on its own; the borough-side rungs are the swap plus a team that gets back up when he does.

characters.name: Tabitha
characters.backstory:
Tabitha turned up at the Festival Green with a borrowed camera and stayed long after everyone else's memory of the day had gone soft, because hers hadn't: the borough started asking her for prints before it occurred to her to charge for them. She shoots the regatta, the festival, whatever Cassadee has running on a given night, and increasingly the open mic room itself, from a stool at the back where Thistle also stands.

What sets her apart from every other animal with a camera in the First Boroughs is that she does not merely point it. Sota's bench at the Observatory took her in for two winters running, grinding glass and arguing about focal length, and Tabitha came out the other side able to say exactly why a lens does what it does — which means she can also tell you exactly why it is about to fail her mid-shoot, and fix it before it does. She still turns up to every hall in town camera first, but she is the only entertainer in the borough who could, if pressed, build the instrument from the bench up.

Her actual ambition outgrew the still frame years ago. She wants to make films — real ones, with a story and a running length — and the borough is not quite big enough yet to give her one, so she practices on everything: Oatmeal's band, Gabe's puppet shows, the regatta's called starts. She is wicked smart about it in a way that unsettles the animals who think a camera operator just points and shoots; ask her why a shot works and she will actually tell you, at length, whether you wanted the answer or not.
characters.voice: Fast, technical, and only occasionally aware she has lost the room. Narrates her own camera settings out loud, to nobody.
characters.arc: The cheap Tabithas are hired hands with the camera doing what somebody else asked; the dear ones have learned exactly how the instrument works and use that to call an opponent's animal back onto the clock before it's ready — a director shouting 'action' on somebody else's set.

characters.name: Taco
characters.backstory:
Taco cooks on a cart at the ferry steps and keeps the hours the river keeps, which is to say no hours at all. Lightermen come off a boat at four in the morning wanting something hot and Taco is there with it; the cart is shut at noon when everybody else's is busiest, and open again when the evening boats come down.

He is an Otter and cannot stand still, so the cart moves too — steps, Boat Shed, the top of the lane — and the river trade finds it anyway, every time, by a method nobody has ever explained to a landsman.
characters.voice: Fast, cheerful, several things at once. Asks how the run went before he asks what you want.
characters.arc: Cart Cook (1) is the pan and somebody else's cart; Quayside Cook (3) is his cart, his hours and the whole river trade's supper. Both do nothing but feed animals, which on the steps at four in the morning is the entire job.

characters.name: Teresa
characters.backstory:
Teresa coaches the borough side and Teresa has no inside voice. What confuses animals who have not met her is that almost everything she bellows is encouraging. WONDERFUL. THAT IS THE IDEA. GOOD LAD. It arrives at the volume of a complaint and it is, without exception, praise, and new players spend about a fortnight braced for a criticism that is never coming.

She is a Mouse, so the side's paperwork is immaculate: fixtures, registrations, the appeal against the county's ruling on the ferry-day postponement, all of it filed and all of it won. She runs training the way she runs the file — everybody works, nobody is spare, and if she has asked more of you this week than last week that is not an accident.

The peppers are the other half. She grows them at the far end of the Allotment Strip, an unreasonable number of varieties, and sells them at the farmer's market on a trestle next to Shay's paintings. She is much quieter at the market. Not quiet. Quieter. And whatever she takes out of the side in a season, she puts back in twice over, which is the only thing about her that she has never once said out loud.
characters.voice: CAPITALS, and kind. The volume is not an opinion; it is just the volume.
characters.arc: Every rung of the coaching track works the other town harder and works her harder still. The peppers are the quiet rungs in between, and they are where the Mouse paperwork lives.

Everything Scott prints about a real animal or a real year goes across Ned's shelves first, and Ned certifies it or Scott cuts it; in fifteen years Lynnette has never printed a correction to a word of his. The other half of Scott's shelf is invention, and it is not kept separate.

Three accounts on the certified half arrived at the print shop finished, on paper Annabelle pulled out of the Salvage Yard before the weather got at it, in a hand nobody has placed. Ned certified all three: names, dates, the year the bridge went, all of it right, including two details the ward records confirm and nobody outside the ward office had cause to know. Scott has never claimed them and has never taken them off the shelf.
characters.voice: None recorded. The dates are given the long way round, the way an animal writes who has been corrected once.
characters.arc: One rung, at Journeyman: a hand Ned will certify is not a hand that learned this week.

Tuppence buys from them without querying the price, which is not like Tuppence; the Counting House stopped querying Tuppence's prices some time ago, which is not like the Counting House. Patch, who judges things for a living and is right, was brought a box off that cloak once and said it was worth keeping.

Thistle has never looked back at a row in his life and so is, by his own account, the last animal in the borough who could tell you anything about it. The reclaimed strip along the far hedgerow is Betty's and was sold on years ago; the field in question is the grange's, and it came in four days early.

On four Wednesdays over two years the queue moved at a speed the counter has never otherwise managed, worked by a clerk in the second window that the ward office does not staff and cannot account for. Marmalade hands his bread out to the kittens first and usually before it is paid for, so a second pair of paws doing the same thing without being asked did not strike him as worth reporting. Ned would not leave the fortnight blank and would not invent a name for it, so the ward record says what the ward saw: the masked otter, the counter, fourteen days. That entry has been corrected twice in thirty years, both times when an otter the borough did know turned out to have been the one standing there.

Rosabeth sings to her plants in full view and has for thirty years, and says only that the singing did not stop while the raccoon was there and the raccoon did not once look up. When the Hiring Hall asked, she gave them the work and not the animal, and Ned wrote down what he was given.

Sage keeps the borough's sky watch and was not there; the two of them work the same bench for whole nights without either saying anything the other wants to hear, and neither has ever suggested a different arrangement. The other has been turning up in the same folder for six years, from a hide on the far bank that Bella did not build, with counts she says are better than hers because whoever took them was willing to be out there at the worst hour of the worst night of it.

She has never mentioned it to anybody except Ned, in the way she has never mentioned the other thing she knows about that room, and the entry in the ward record is four words long.

Berry was three streets away with the Town Clock stopped and did not get back until dark. Everything on the bench was mended, by the animals who brought it, and Berry — who taught Moss at twelve and is still the one animal Moss listens to — went along the row, looked at each one, and said that whoever it was had done it properly.

Taco's answer, given to Brooke and to the Hiring Hall and to Ned in identical words, is that the cart was open and the food was good. There is a line in the returns column that has been paid every autumn for eleven years and has nothing in the name column. Two packets, always, of whatever was taken, dry and clean and better than what went out. Maribel has filed the objection to a hedgerow being taken down twice and had it thrown out twice, so she is not an animal who lets a form go unfinished; this one she leaves.

Andrew keeps the Lending Library's late desk and copies out by hand what cannot be lent, a page or two a night, so that there is a second one. Twice now he has come in to find the night's pages already done, in a hand that is not his and is better than his, and the book squared away on the shelf it came off.

The Library has twice filed Andrew's copy as the original, which is a joke the borough enjoys; it has never worked out what to do about these. Lynnette will not print a claim Ned cannot certify and Ned will not certify a hand without an animal attached to it, so the pages sit in the stack unsigned and everybody uses them.

characters.arc: One rung. Whoever was at the shelves is somebody the Library already knows; it simply does not know which one.

What it wants is the work in full and the animal in shadow — a hood, a scarf, a coat collar, the light on the job and not on whoever is doing it — so that the card reads as the entry in Ned's unsigned column that it is.

characters.name: The Veiled Wright
characters.backstory:
Hoot keeps the ward's keys and a standing list of animals who have asked to be woken, and knocks at four in the morning on anybody who is on it. Being woken in the First Boroughs is a service you sign up for. Nobody signs up to have the sash cord replaced while they sleep, and yet.

It is a small and specific list: a sash cord, a dropped gate hinge, a pump handle, a stair tread, each done overnight in a ward where somebody had complained about it out loud the previous day. Berry's position is that the work is good and that it is not hers. Moss's position, which cost him a formal warning at Velvet's counter for something unrelated, is that it is not his either and that whoever it is does not foul a hitch.
characters.voice: None recorded. Nothing has ever been left behind but the shavings, swept.
characters.arc: One rung, at cost 0, because this is an animal the borough has never yet paid.

wantedArt.why: An obscured figure has no face and no painted tile of their own; this card stands on a borrowed scene of the right work. What it wants is the work in full and the animal in shadow — a hood, a scarf, a coat collar, the light on the job and not on whoever is doing it — so that the card reads as the entry in Ned's unsigned column that it is.

characters.name: Thistle
characters.backstory:
Thistle works, and that is nearly the whole of what the borough can tell you about him. Up before the lanterns, home after the moon, thirty-odd years of it, and in all that time nobody has had a word out of him that was not about the job or worth hearing. He is not shy and he is not sullen. He simply does not see why a thing that can be done should be discussed first.

What he is actually for, the grange worked out early and has never said to his face: put Thistle at the head of a row and the row keeps his pace. Not because he drives it — he has never once looked back — but because the pace is exactly right, and an animal who falls in behind him comes off that field at dusk having done half again what they meant to and not feeling it until the morning. The grange sends him out with the ones who think they are no good. It works about nine times in ten, and the tenth is usually a fox.

And there is the other thing. Two evenings a month, in whatever room is having the open mic, there is a badger at the back by the door who does not take his coat off, does not drink anything, listens to one singer's set with his eyes shut, and is gone before the applause. Cassadee keeps the list and knows exactly which nights he comes, and has never mentioned it to him, and has twice moved that singer up the running order so he would not have to stay so late. The borough has decided, collectively and without discussion, that this is nobody's business. It is the only thing about Thistle anybody gossips about, and they do it very quietly.
characters.voice: Short. Answers the question asked. Long silences that are not uncomfortable unless you make them so. The most he has ever said at once was about drainage.
characters.arc: Five rungs at one pace. The Almanac Keeper at 1 is the Badger signature: the town braces and the weather goes over it. The Field Hand at 2 pays his own next shift better; the Grange Warden at 3 starts paying for everybody's. The Field Surveyor at 4 and the Grange Elder at 5 are the thing the grange actually worked out — while Thistle is standing there, every shift the town finishes is worth more, and at the top it is worth two more, which is thirty years of pace made into a rate.

characters.name: Tuppence
characters.backstory:
Tuppence comes out from the Capital City about once a month with a cart, and what is on the cart is the best hour in the borough. Nobody, including Tuppence, can always say what the things are. There is a brass object with a hinge. There is a crate of the ribbed glass that the Observatory later turned out to want very badly. There is a coil of something that Moss looked at for a long minute, bought the whole of, and used on a bridge arch, and which the Capital City's guild has since written to ask about.

The trade is not junk and it is not antiques. Tuppence buys ahead of the borough's understanding — the fittings, the stuff, the odd modern material that nobody here has a use for yet — and then waits, which is the most Squirrel thing about them and the reason they are never quite as poor as the cart looks. Half of what is screwed, hung, glazed or bolted into the First Boroughs' Buildings came off that cart at a price the Counting House still does not believe, and the standing joke at the Counting House is that Tuppence's invoices are cheaper than the queries about them.

They and Hazel have the obvious arrangement: what the day market cannot name goes to the night market, where not being able to name a thing is the whole appeal. Patch is the other end of it — animals bring Patch a thing and ask whether it is worth keeping, and about four times a year the thing turns out to have come off Tuppence's cart, and Patch says yes, and does not explain why.
characters.voice: Cheerful, vague about provenance, precise about price. "I don't know what it is either. It's four Supply, and you'll want two."
characters.arc: One rung, hired out of the Capital City, because the cart only ever comes out once a month. It does two things at once, which is the whole trade: a Building goes up cheaper while Tuppence is in town, and what they make on the shift goes under the cart rather than into the till.

characters.name: Velvet
characters.backstory:
Velvet is a government cat. His mother was a government cat and her mother kept the Capital City's tithe rolls, and Velvet has never once in his life wanted to be anything else, which the borough finds faintly alarming and Velvet finds restful. He came out to the First Boroughs as a petition runner at seventeen and has been behind one counter or another ever since.

What he holds now is the consents. Nothing goes up in this town and nothing comes down without a form Velvet has read aloud to somebody, slowly, all of it, while they fidget. Ned keeps the ward records and Velvet keeps the consents; they are different shelves and in fifteen years the two have never disagreed, which both of them regard as ordinary and everybody else regards as slightly eerie. Moss's formal warning from the Capital City came across Velvet's counter, and Velvet read that aloud too, at the same pace, to a badger who wanted to be anywhere else in the world.

The thing to understand about him is that he is not enduring any of this. He loves it. He loves the mundane — a well-ruled column, a fee scale that comes out even, a Tuesday. He loves patterns, and he sees them, which is why he is the animal who noticed the far hedgerow appearing in three unrelated files in one spring and said so before anybody else had. And he loves the queue: the small talk while a long form is filled in is, he has said in a public meeting, the best part of his week. The borough was startled, thought about it, and decided to believe him.
characters.voice: Unhurried, kind, faintly pleased. Reads things aloud in full. Asks after your aunt while the ink dries, and remembers the answer next quarter.
characters.arc: Five rungs and one counter, going from the form to the fabric of the town. The Counter Clerk at 1 gets one Building through cheaper. The Notary at 2 is the Cat signature: he gets up when the small print says he may. The Neighborhood Registrar at 3 runs the discount every morning. Then the other half of the office opens: the Surveyor of Works at 4 takes a Building down and puts a discarded one up in its place, and the Clerk of the Works at 5 does both — the rate and the demolition order — which is the whole consents shelf in one animal.

wantedArt.why: The Surveyor of Works is outdoors for once: a cat in a good coat with a clipboard, in front of something about to come down. It carries whiskerwood/4, the counter portrait, as a stand-in.

wantedVerbs.verb: buildingsAtLeast as a scaling condition on a discount
wantedVerbs.why: The story wanted the rate to read as an office that gets better at its own job — the more this town has raised, the cheaper the next consent. `buildingsAtLeast` exists as a yes/no condition, but nothing scales a mod's value by a count.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Two flat rates on two rungs: 1 less at the Registrar, 2 less at the Clerk of the Works. The office gets better because Velvet is promoted, not because the town got bigger.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: a mod's value may be counted rather than printed. `addMod` takes `valuePer: "buildingsBuilt"` and a `max`, so a rate can scale with what the town has actually raised. The Clerk of the Works is 1 off every Building and 1 more for each one already standing, up to 3 more: the office gets better at its own job, which is what the story asked for. The Registrar below him stays a flat rate, because he is a promotion away from the counting.

characters.name: Willow
characters.backstory:
Willow started with one ferry. She was nineteen, it was not a good ferry, and she talked the previous owner into terms that he described for years afterwards as generous of him. She now signs for everything that floats between the ferry steps and the county line, and for a good deal that does not: the boat yard, the two rows of cottages on the towpath, the lease on the arcade, the whole of the harbour office. She sells big. She has never in her life sold anybody a small thing, and the borough is not certain she knows how.

What she is, technically, is the Harbourmaster, which means the River Otter licence is granted out of her office, and the river trade's whole ladder — dock hand, ferry hand, lighterman, wright — runs up to a desk she sits behind. Brooke has been about two years off it for eight years and knows exactly whose desk that is. Willow is not unfair about it. She is simply the largest fact in that room, and she takes up all of it, and she talks.

The talking is the thing. She is the best talker in the First Boroughs and the borough is proud of her for it in the way you are proud of weather. She does not lie and she does not bully; she arrives at the table having already worked out the two worst outcomes available to you, sets them both down in front of you with enormous warmth, and waits. Animals come away from Willow's table having agreed to the less bad one and feeling, on the walk home, that they chose it. Half the harbour was bought that way. Pebble's family, who have had the crossing for seven generations, have a standing rule about never meeting her without a third animal present, and will not say which year they made it.
characters.voice: Big, warm, expensive. Uses your name twice a sentence. Lays out your options in ascending order of how much she would like you to take the last one.
characters.arc: Five rungs, from one ferry to the whole harbour. The Ferry Trader at 1 and the Tide Reckoner at 3 are Otter tempo — a paw free, a shift moved. From the Toll Keeper at 2 the table starts working on the animal across it: a card of theirs goes back on top of their deck, because whatever they were holding is not the thing they are going to be talking about now. The Harbourmaster at 4 puts both bad outcomes on the table and one of them happens, and the Harbour Admiral at 5 does that every morning and takes a cut of everything the Capital City sells.

wantedArt.why: The Admiral is the office rather than the quay — the leases, the licences, an otter behind a desk too large for the room. It carries neighbors/12, Willow on the quay, as a stand-in.

wantedVerbs.verb: opponentChoice (a rival picks which hardship they take)
wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for a card that makes the other Mayor choose between losing Supply or another hardship. Two things are missing: nothing on a Character can take Supply off a rival at all — `everyoneLosesSupply` is a Disruption's shared shock and `giveSupplyToOpponent` runs the other way — and no effect offers a rival a choice of branches. Every reaching verb in the vocabulary (`makeBusy`, `opponentTopdeckFromHand`, `unemployOpponentCharacter`) simply happens to them.
wantedVerbs.workaround: The choice became a toss. The Harbourmaster and the Harbour Admiral put both bad outcomes on the table with `coinFlip` — an animal goes back to work, or a card goes back on top of the deck — so the pair is real even though the rival does not get to pick which. Roger's ha'penny is the borough's own method for a call that will not come down on its own, which makes the seam a thing the town already does rather than a thing the engine could not do.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built, both halves: `opponentLosesSupply` takes Supply off a rival and tells them it happened (`onSupplyLost` fires for them), and `opponentChoice` puts two branches on the table and lets the rival pick which one they take. The Harbourmaster offers 2 Supply or a card back on top; the Harbour Admiral offers 3 Supply or an animal put back to work. `power.js` pays the card the least of its branches, because the rival picks — which is also the design rule: print two you would be happy with. Roger's ha'penny stays the borough's method for a call nobody will make; this is the harbour office's, which is to make somebody else make it.

characters.name: Winter
characters.backstory:
Before he was the borough's TV scientist, Winter sat the Observatory's selection board twice, same as Comet, and came away both times with a courteous letter and no seat. He took the rejection the way an Owl takes most things: awake, at four in the morning, turning it over until it stopped looking like a loss and started looking like a different job. What the board never gave him was a launch. What it did give him, over two applications and a great deal of reading he was not required to do, was an actual working knowledge of how the sky gets studied — the manifests, the order book, the instruments Sota grinds — and that turned out to be worth more to the borough than the seat would have been.

Now he has the whole town's children believing science is the best thing that happens on a given evening, because he has never once faked understanding something for the sake of a segment. He plans every show himself — the experiment, the running order, the follow-up question a kitten is about to ask — and he plans it because he has actually done the science, not merely reported on animals who have.

He tapes in whatever hall Cassadee will give him, and treats the Capital City's own market days the way Orien treats a set of figures: something to be read closely and rearranged to his advantage before anyone else notices there was an advantage to be had.
characters.voice: Warm on camera, exacting off it. Explains everything twice: once for the room, once correctly.
characters.arc: The cheap Winters are still finding the format; the middle ones have learned to read the Capital City's own market the way they once read the Observatory's manifests; the top one gets the thing he actually wanted, and opens a sixth stall in the display for as long as he's standing at the desk.

wantedVerbs.verb: a card that opens a sixth stall in the Capital City display
wantedVerbs.why: Winter wanted a top card that puts a sixth animal, Building or Ordinance up for bid alongside the usual five, so his show always has one more thing to point at.
wantedVerbs.workaround: capitalCitySize is a fixed rule, not a thing any Character can move, so he cannot add a sixth booth. His top card instead goes as far as the vocabulary allows on the same idea: look at the top three cards of the Market Deck, put them back in whichever order he likes, then send the one he does not want to the bottom — reading and rearranging the market rather than widening it.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as capitalCityExtraStalls, a passive read by both Mayors' abilitySources and summed in state.js's capitalCitySize() — the Capital City's refill target is the printed floor plus whatever either town is carrying. mk_winter_tv_scientist_5 now carries it: while he is upright, the display deals a sixth stall, shared exactly like the other five.

wantedArt.why: No painted tile shows a studio floor or a science segment being taped. All five borrow the Night Skies scene until one is commissioned.

characters.name: Yellow
characters.backstory:
Yellow came up from the suburbs at the edge of the Capital City telling anyone who'd listen exactly how fresh his rhymes were, and arrived in the First Boroughs to find a town with an open mic list, a booker who does not care where you're from, and absolutely no street to speak of. He has not let either fact slow him down. His whole catalogue is built out of what the borough actually has to offer — a verse about the seed bank's open day, four bars about Marmalade's ovens, an entire closing number about peanut butter and pecan pie that has nothing to do with anything and that Cassadee has stopped trying to cut from his set.

Nobody in the First Boroughs is going to mistake him for where he says he's from, and he knows it, and it has never once cost him a booking. Cassadee keeps him on the list because the room likes him, which is the whole of her job description and the only part of it Yellow has ever cared about. He shows up, he raps about pecan pie like it's a grudge, and somehow it works.

What the Hiring Hall has actually noticed about Yellow, over several seasons of watching him, is that he is never between jobs. He has never once turned up in Unemployment, not for a day, not for an hour — whatever else is true about his rhymes, the borough has never had cause to wonder where he is.
characters.voice: Loud, proud, entirely unbothered by the gap between the persona and the postcode. Works 'suburbs' and 'pecan pie' into everything, unironically.
characters.arc: Priced differently for what they actually promise: the cheap one shelters him the week he arrives, the way any protected animal is sheltered, until your next turn. The dear one doesn't need the shelter renewed, because he simply does not go to Unemployment, full stop.

wantedVerbs.why: Yellow's story says he simply never goes to Unemployment, full stop, not 'until your next turn'.
wantedVerbs.workaround: protectCharacter, run once on recruit and then again every onTurnStart, keeps him out of reach of an opponent's effects and of the shared shocks that send both towns to Unemployment — the nearest the vocabulary gets to 'never', short of a card that reads the Unemployment phase itself.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as immuneToUnemployment, a fact printed on the card and checked once, at the top of unemployStack() in effects.js, before anything that can lapse — not a mod, not a shelter with a turn number on it. mk_yellow_freshest_thing_4 now carries it and is exactly as permanent as the story says.

wantedArt.why: No painted tile shows a rapper at the open mic. Both borrow the plain Squirrel scene until one is commissioned.

characters.name: Cindy
characters.backstory:
Cindy sits in the ward court, which is one room over the old assize office with a window that does not shut and a bench somebody made too high. She came up through it the long way — usher, clerk, magistrate — and she has heard every version of every story the First Boroughs has to tell, most of them twice, a good many of them from the same animal on two different days.

What she is known for is the stare. Cindy asks a question, and then she waits, and the waiting is the whole method: she does not fill the silence, she does not help, and she does not look away. The borough's own view is that nobody has ever got a lie all the way across that bench. She would say it is not a trick and that animals mostly want to tell the truth and only need to be given long enough to get round to it.

What she will not have is a smart mouth. An animal who comes in clever gets put straight back to work — she has adjourned a hearing for a fortnight over one remark and made the whole yard wait on it. And she is fair, which in a Fox is the thing the borough finds hardest to credit and the thing she is proudest of: she hears both sides all the way to the end, including the side she stopped believing in the first five minutes.
characters.voice: Level, unhurried, and comfortable with a silence other animals are not. Asks short questions. Says 'take your time' and means the opposite of what it sounds like.
characters.arc: Four rungs of one career, and the same animal at each of them. The Clerk at 1 only reads the room — the Fox charter's looking, done as a court's paperwork. The Magistrate at 2 does something about what she reads: the clever answer goes back to work. The Circuit Judge at 4 is the fairness printed as a rule — her challenges win ties, and a rival who challenges her pays her for the privilege of being heard. The Justice at 5 is all of it at once, plus the one thing only she does: she puts the ruling to the rival and lets them pick which way they would rather have it, which is what seeing both sides looks like from the other side of the bench.

characters.name: Elvira
characters.backstory:
Elvira reads futures. She started at the fairground with a card table and a cloth over it, and she is still at the fairground most weeks, though the booth has a roof now and a queue that starts before she does.

She is right often enough that the borough has stopped being able to laugh it off, and wrong often enough that nobody can quite call it a trade. The awkward part is how specific she is. She told Pebble there would be water in the cellar on a Thursday and there was, three Thursdays later. She told half the open mic list that something would go wrong with a candle, which everybody ignored until Jim's hair grew back wrong. She also told the ferry office there was danger on the water for a fortnight and there was no danger on the water for a fortnight, and the ferry office has not entirely forgiven her.

What she is never wrong about is the mood. Elvira reads for animals who have had a hard season, and whatever the cards say she sends them out of the booth better than they came in — which she will tell you, cheerfully, is the actual job, and the futures are what gets them through the door. She is a Cat about the rest of it: she turns up when she turns up, reads for whom she pleases, and is unbothered that a false warning about danger is not, on the whole, a comfort.
characters.voice: Warm, bright, and entirely unembarrassed. Delivers a catastrophe and a compliment in the same breath. 'Oh, that's a bad card, love — you'll be fine.'
characters.arc: Four windows and a coin. The Tea-Leaf Reader at 0 reads her own cards; the Fairground Booth at 2 reads the Capital City's, or the rival's, on the toss; the Fortune Teller at 3 is the half of the job she is actually good at — she pays out when the season has gone against you; the Reader of the Long Odds at 4 is all three windows at once and the Cat signature under it, because she gets up when she feels like getting up.

wantedVerbs.why: The booth reads three futures — yours, the Capital City's and the rival's — and the engine could see the first two and not the third.
wantedVerbs.workaround: None needed.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built for this batch (v0.14.0). `peekOpponentDeck` looks at the top cards of the rival's deck; information only, and the rival is told, the same manners `peekOpponentHand` keeps. Elvira's cost-0, cost-2 and cost-4 cards all reach it on the losing side of a coin.

characters.name: Jim
characters.backstory:
Jim writes a blog nobody asked for about a company nobody in the First Boroughs had heard of until he started. It is called the same thing it has always been called, it goes out whenever he finishes it, and the borough reads it — partly because he is a genuinely good explainer of how a thing works, and partly to find out what he has bought this week.

He has bought everything. The self-winding shutters, the pocket abacus that does not work in the damp, the automated candle on launch day, which is why there is a patch on the left side of his head where the fur came back in a different colour and never went back to the first one. Jim shows it to visitors. He is not embarrassed about the candle; he is embarrassed that he waited two days for the second batch.

He programs, in the way Raccoons program — out of whatever was in the bin behind the works, at four in the morning, extremely well. What he actually is, underneath the queueing and the merchandise, is an animal who believes the future is going to be better than this and wants to be there when it starts. The borough finds this either charming or exhausting, usually depending on how recently he has explained something.
characters.voice: Fast, delighted, and forty words past the point. Opens with 'okay so'. Has a strong view on a thing he has owned for four hours.
characters.arc: Every rung of Jim turns Supply into cards, because that is what he does with money. The Blogger at 0 and the Programmer at 2 buy a card or two at the counter. The Early Adopter at 4 pays the launch-day price for the privilege of having it first. The Fanboy at 5 queues all night and is not in a fit state to work afterwards — he draws more cards for the price than anything else in the collection, and then he goes to Unemployment, which is the joke the borough has been making about him for years and is finally printed.

characters.name: Robbie
characters.backstory:
Robbie reports for the borough paper, which is four sheets and a Thursday, and he has never filed a clean headline in his life. The drainage review was DOWN THE PLUGHOLE. The bridge inquiry was A SPAN OF ATTENTION. He laughed at both of them in the office, alone, for some time.

Nobody else laughs much, and it has never once slowed him down. He is entirely happy being the only animal in the room who finds it funny, and he has the Badger's gift for simply still being there: he outlasts a meeting, he outlasts a denial, and he is at the back of the ward hall at half past eleven with his notebook out when everybody who came to watch has gone home.

The suits are the other thing. Robbie wears patterns that should not exist — a check that has an argument in it, something in ochre with a repeating pheasant — and no animal in either borough has ever found out where they come from. He deflects the question with a pun every time, which the borough now believes is the point. What he is actually good at is knowing what is coming into the Capital City before it is put up, and saying so in print, which is a kind of power the auction house has never worked out how to take off him.
characters.voice: Cheerful, punning, and unbothered by silence after a joke. Says 'you'll like this one' and is always wrong about that.
characters.arc: Five rungs of the same notebook, and the market gets easier to read at each one. The Cub Reporter at 0 only looks at what is coming; the Columnist at 1 puts it back in the order he wants it in; the Features Writer at 2 does it off a Busy shift, which is the paper coming out whether or not he stood up. The Editor at 3 is the Badger signature in print — the shared shock that lands on both towns goes in the spike and does not land on his. The Editor-in-Chief at 5 reads three deep, sinks a lot to the bottom of the Market Deck where nobody bids on it this year, and still spikes the weather.

characters.name: Cornelius
characters.backstory:
Cornelius runs FutureTech, and the Capital City retains him whenever the books will not balance, which is more often than the Capital City says out loud. He arrives with three automatons and a folder, talks for forty minutes without appearing to breathe, and leaves the ward with a schedule that works, a roof that went up for nothing, and a faint sense of having agreed to something it cannot now find in writing.

He is, by every account, brilliant. The costings are right. The buildings do go up cheaper. The automatons — a different one most weeks, each better than the last — do the work of four animals and do not complain about the weather, and Cornelius is genuinely, visibly delighted by every one of them.

Nobody knows where they go afterwards. A machine that was on the site on Friday is not on the site on Monday and is not in the yard, the store or the scrap. Robbie has asked him about it in print four times. Cornelius answers a different question each time, warmly, at length, and with figures, and the borough comes away having learned a great deal about something else.
characters.voice: Loud, fast, relentlessly pleased. Talks in numbers and slogans at once. 'Right — right — so here's the thing, and this is the exciting bit.'
characters.arc: One card, hired out of the Capital City for a season, because that is how the borough gets him: a contract, a discount on everything with a roof on it, and a folder of costings left behind when he goes. He does not stay, and the automatons do not stay either.

wantedVerbs.why: The pitch is that FutureTech gets the roof up for nothing, and the story wanted a Building simply raised.
wantedVerbs.workaround: A standing `buildingDiscount` of 3 and a `lotDiscount` of 2 on every lot with a roof on it, which is the same bargain paid in instalments.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Deliberately not built: a Building that appears without an auction or a crew would be the one card in the collection that skips both, and the discounts already make him the cheapest roof in the game.

characters.name: Henrietta
characters.backstory:
Henrietta runs the front desk at the Hiring Hall, which means she runs the board, the queue and, by her own account, most of what anybody in the borough knows about anybody else. She took the desk over from nobody in particular — it was simply there, and she was better at it than whoever had it before — and she has not stopped talking since, in the friendliest possible way, to every animal who has ever stood in that queue.

She is, by universal agreement, the best-informed animal in either borough, and also the least reliable, because Henrietta does not distinguish between a fact and a good story the way the rest of the Hiring Hall would like her to. She will tell you exactly as much about the animal three places ahead of you in the queue as she will about a character in one of Lynnette's water-stained novels, in the same breath, at the same volume, with the same conviction that you needed to know. Nobody has ever caught her being unkind about it. She simply cannot tell where the gossip stops and the town starts, and has decided this is everybody else's problem to sort out, not hers.

What she is genuinely good at, underneath all of it, is placing a Rabbit. She knows every warren, every cousin, every animal who owes another animal a favour, and when a good one comes through the door she does not merely post the job — she works the whole room until the hire happens, and the better the job, the harder she works it.
characters.voice: Fast, warm, and unable to finish a sentence about the weather without mentioning three animals by name. Never malicious, never quite on topic.
characters.arc: The Front Desk Clerk at 0 does what the desk is actually for — a name on the board, a small nudge. The Placement Officer at 2 works a room for an afternoon. The Head of Rabbit Recruitment at 4 has stopped pretending it is only paperwork: she gets on the warren telegraph and does not stop until the best Rabbit in three wards is standing in your town.

wantedVerbs.verb: a bonus scaled to the exact cost of the Character just recruited
wantedVerbs.why: The story wants Henrietta's help to keep paying out better the pricier the Rabbit she places — a smooth curve, not three steps of it.
wantedVerbs.workaround: No engine rate reads the cost of the specific card a `recruitFromHand` rider just brought in (`addMod`'s `valuePer` only counts `buildingsBuilt` or heads in town). Built instead as three versions, each opening the door to pricier Rabbits than the last and paying more when one comes through it — the arc does in three rungs what a single scaled card would do in one.

characters.name: Balto
characters.backstory:
Balto has been making furniture longer than most of the Town Workshop's current bench has been standing, and he is still the one animal in it who can be woken at any hour of the night by a knock on the door and a wobbling table leg. He works the way Owls work — through the dark, unhurried, with everybody else's shift asleep around him — and by the time the borough is up he has usually already been round to see what needed doing.

His hands are enormous for his size and steadier than they have any right to be at his age; ask him and he will tell you it is fifty years of dovetails and nothing more mysterious than that. He built half the benches at Berry's tool-lending day, the long table in the Open Mic Room, and the shelf under the Lending Library's low window that Sage still reads at. None of it was commissioned. He simply noticed a shelf was wanted and turned up with the wood.

Later in life he opened a small shop off the Town Workshop court to sell what he could not give away fast enough, and found, to his mild surprise, that he was good at that too — an Owl who reads a room at four in the morning reads a customer at noon without much trouble. He still does both jobs, in the same order every night: the neighbor first, the counter second.
characters.voice: Slow, dry, and kind without ever sounding like it is trying to be. Measures twice, says less.
characters.arc: The Bench Owl at 0 is a night visit with a bag of tools. The Cabinetmaker at 1 does the same, better. The Shopkeeper at 2 has started charging for some of it. The Furniture Craftsman at 3 is the name half the borough's good chairs go under. The Guild Furniture Broker at 5 sells what he cannot make fast enough and is generous with the credit either way — Owl and Badger alike leave his counter with something extra, because he has never once, in fifty years, sent a neighbor home short.

characters.name: Fingers
characters.backstory:
Nobody in either borough can say for certain how Fingers gets where he gets. He has been seen coming down off the Observatory dome, coming up out of a cellar he had no key to, and standing in a queue that had not existed thirty seconds before — climbing, diving, picking a lock that everyone agrees should not have been pickable, or simply walking in the front door as if that had been an option the whole time.
